subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil). The Hon. Member has had extensive experience in banking. He carries a law degree and is also a farmer. It is very thrilling to see the emphasis which the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw puts on farming. I enjoyed his remarks very much indeed but the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw did not have time to deal with the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. Does he have any suggestions as to how we can make the Western Grain Stabilization Fund a little more palatable to the western Members?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the present time the Western Grain Stabilization Fund pay-out is based on a five-year average. It does not appear there will be a pay-out this year. The farmers in the west are suffering from financial difficulties because of low grain prices and high input costs. If the Government were prepared to bring in an amendment to the Act which would base a pay-out on a three-year average rather than a five-year average, there would probably be a payment of $150 million this year which would be quite an injection of money into the economy of western Canada. This would not only help the farmers but the machinery dealers and the whole economy of western Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not have a further question for the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw but because of his extensive knowledge of agricultural matters I would like his comment. At the present time many farmers in the Province of Alberta, I suppose all through western Canada and perhaps right across Canada, are having such a difficult time on the
land that they are taking other jobs to keep their farms viable and ongoing. When a farmer works out he puts himself in a position under the Income Tax Act where he can claim only a $5,000 loss. Does the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw have any suggestions with regard to the Income Tax section?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it appears to me that many of the farmers who are taking extra jobs are doing so because they are having difficulty meeting their financial commitments. It would require just a simple amendment to the Income Tax Act to enable farmers to benefit from the write-offs of their usual expenses in farming. I can understand the situation of hobby farmers not being entitled to claim their full deduction of expenses in their farming operations, but certainly where a bona fide farmer is doing his utmost to raise money to keep his farming operation going, the Government, I think, is obligated to bring in the necessary amendment to enable him to write off his normal expenses.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a privilege to rise today to express my support, optimism and enthusiasm for the budget which was presented in the House by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde). The budget offers strong medicine, not only to deal with the acute problem of unemployment today, but also with the chronic problem of slow productivity growth that Canada has experienced over the past decade.
Technology development is central to both these issues. I am confident that the proposals I present today for a technology policy for Canada will restore our ability to confront the demands of the 1990s with a healthy, productive and vigorous economy. I am pleased that the budget has dedicated over $700 million for technology development in the next two years. Never in the history of the country has such an effort been made to enhance the Canadian technology base.
Technology is changing many dimensions of our lives at an unprecedented pace. Communications, automation, new materials and consumer electronics are all having a profound effect on our livelihoods and on our view of the world. Some of

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
these changes we welcome; some we resist. But either way they represent a force that we cannot ignore.

Technological innovation in the work place may create new jobs and new wealth, but it may also eliminate existing jobs. This Government is determined to show leadership in supporting the development of new technology that will be to Canada's best advantage. We are also determined to have all Canadians share in the benefits that new technologies will bring. Changes are always upsetting and can often be painful. On the other hand, we must realize that we have no choice. We must keep pace with developments and change when the world changes. If we want to continue to enjoy the high standard of living we have today, we must be ready for the opportunities tomorrow will bring. Canada is not the only country that is faced with this climate of uncertainty.

At the Economic Summit held last June in Versailles, this issue was of such priority that a special working group was established to address the world-wide concern about technological change and development. The group reached a consensus on many issues, especially on the awareness of the profound effects of technological change on all nations. Its final report emphasized the theme that technology, while not a panacea for our economic ills, is a powerful instrument which can forge a better future for us and for our children.
Any period of transition such as the one we are now experiencing through technological change is exacting and stressful. The working group emphasized the need for a special program to promote the flexibility, adaptability and mobility of labour. Its report is optimistic that technological innovation will build the jobs of tomorrow. Canada has been quick to respond to this challenge, and, over the past few months we have been examining how a technology policy can best work for us. We have had to take a hard look at the nature of technology itself and to take an equally hard look at how technology interacts with our Government and with our economy.
Technology is all-pervasive. It touches each and every aspect of our lives. Any policy that addresses technology development must recognize this. To be fully effective, a technology policy for Canada has to act with and through economic, fiscal and industrial policies. Technological advances give the lifeblood to our manufacturing and resource industries, but a technology policy also has to influence, and be influenced by, our social policies. It has a profound effect on employment, our health, our environment and even our general lifestyles.
Nor can technology policy be considered in isolation from science policy. The basic research fundamental to scientific progress has often provided the inspirational source for remarkable leaps in technological development. The time has passed when we can comfortably address each of these areas separately. If we are to compete in this increasingly competitive world, and still maintain our standing of living, we must
have a forum that can address technology development as an integrated policy with separate but synergistic components.
Because, as I said, science policy and technology are allpervasive and because at the federal level science and technology range across programs in all major Departments-Communications, Environment, Agriculture, Energy, Fisheries, Health and Welfare, National Research Council, to name a few-I am pleased to report that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has established a special subcommittee of Cabinet on technology development which will be dedicated to achieving the integration of policy elements and to advancing technology development in all sectors. Each Minister of the subcommittee has the authority, the resources and the influence to bring about the required changes through creating new programs or through adapting existing ones to specific policy areas. Each Minister contributes a unique and essential point of view to the continuing development of a technology policy for Canada.
The first task of the subcommittee has been to confirm our policy direction for technology development in Canada. This has been done. Our objectives are set. Indeed, some of these objectives have already been translated into action in the budget. We have also, however, established a policy framework which will maintain the budget momentum, guide our progress and concentrate our energies on long-term objectives. It is this technology policy which I would like to present to my colleagues in the House of Commons today.
The first objective of the technology policy is to strengthen the Canadian economy through the creation, application and diffusion of state of the art technologies. Second, we intend to manage the process of technological development so that Canadians are aware both of the opportunities and the problems that may arise. Well-informed Canadians will make the right choices for themselves and for this country. Third, we must ensure that the benefits of technology development are shared equitably among all Canadians in every region. Last, but by no means least, we must encourage a social climate that places a premium on scientific and technological excellence, curiosity and innovation. These are the values that will guarantee our progress.
[ Translation]
These are the general objectives for technology development in Canada and they set the parameters of the party by which we shall be guided. A detailed technology policy, however, must also consider the contribution that each sector of our society can make to technology development and the impact of technological change on every aspect of our lives. In this respect, the Federal Government has specifically defined the objectives related to each particular sector. Here are a few of the objectives that illustrate the extent of the present Government's commitment to our technological future.

Our objectives relating to the business sector reflect the primacy of the private sector in initiating innovation and new
May 3, 1983

investment. We will support the initiatives of the private sector by encouraging an over-all business environment that supports investment, innovation and enterprise. Our commitment here can be seen in the tax structure we have established to encourage investment in research and innovation. Canadian tax incentives for research and development, even before this budget, have been among the world's richest. We can look at Japan, West Germany, United States, France, Great Britain or Sweden and we find that, with the single exception of Singapore, Canada has the most beneficial over-all tax structure for research and development. Tax benefits for industry in terms of forgone revenue to the Government are calculated to be over $200 million in 1983.
The budget has significantly enriched this package. It has, for example, introduced important changes to the investment tax credit which will particularly benefit small firms and significantly broaden the application of the tax credits. The budget has also made proposals which, as a former tax lawyer, I am particularly pleased to see as they simplify the research and development tax incentives and make them more effective. These proposals are expected to contribute a further $100 million in industrial incentives for research and development. They have been put forward in the form of a paper for consultation which calls for comments by July 1, 1983, to ensure early implementation of the proposals.
Another federal Government objective in relation to the business sector will ensure that current industrial support programs for technology development continue to be effective and that Canadian firms have access to the most productive, up to date technologies available. In support of this objective, the Government will spend $20 million over the next two years to expand the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program. In particular, the Field Advisory Service and the Technical Information Service will now expand their current services to include small and mediumsized businesses, greatly assisting the diffusion of needed technologies to all companies across Canada. This is one part of the $100 million that the Government has committed to new technology initiatives over the next two years.

As far as labour is concerned, the federal Government's main objectives concern our ability to predict the effects of technological change in order to minimize its negative aspects. Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that most people will welcome the realization that new technologies will do away with many boring and repetitive tasks. I have every reason to believe that people are eagerly waiting for a chance to get one of the interesting and better-paid jobs that will be created as a result of new technologies. In fact, under the heading of training assistance, the Budget has earmarked an additional $155 million for human resource development programs.
The Budget-Mr. Johnston

Another objective of our technology policy is to encourage labour-management mechanisms on all levels to encourage joint planning for technological change. We will also support organized labour in its study of issues brought about by this change and its preparation and efforts to deal with them. The federal Government has approved $10 million to be spent over the next two years to encourage business and labour to establish a centre for productivity and employment growth. Negotiations with respect to the establishment of this centre will be led by my colleagues, the Hon. Charles Caccia, Minister of Labour, and the Hon. Ed Lumley, Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
The federal Government would also like to foster a core of excellence within the university structure which conducts research relevant to industry. To support university research and enhance its contribution to technology development, the federal Government will increase the funding of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council by almost $27 million over the next two years.
It is also an objective of our technology policy that industry become more aware of the research done in universities, and at the same time that science in the universities and federal laboratories be better attuned to the opportunities in the industrial world. The federal Government will spend $9 million over the next two years to strengthen joint university-industry research and technology efforts.
[ Translation]
This Government intends to make sure that R&D carried out in federal laboratories will support the requirements of industry within the framework of our economic objectives. Our programs and policies will be designed in accordance with these objectives. We shall be examining federal research programs to find out whether there are certain areas in which they could be better attuned to the needs of industry. The communications sector is one in which we are particularly interested. Canada has a world reputation for excellence in this field, and so that we may continue in this direction, my colleague, the Hon. Francis Fox, who is in the House today, the Minister of Communications-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order! This is the second time the Hon. Minister has mentioned the name of one of his colleagues in the House. I must remind him that he should refer to his hon. colleagues by their title, the name of their riding or their position and not by their own name.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I apologize, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), who is in the House right now, has proposed establishing a non-profit corporation that would belong to the Government and others and would carry out R&D in the related fields of telecommunications, space technology and information processing. A task force, consisting of representatives from industry, the universities, and Government, will be established to assess the

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
viability of this proposal. We have earmarked $250,000 for conducting this study.
The federal Government is also determined that Canada meet the challenge of the emerging new technologies.
To make sure that Canada benefits fully from new developments in the increasingly important field of biotechnology, the federal Government is committing $22 million toward implementing a national biotechnology strategy. This strategy will support research networks-involving Government, universities and industry-which will concentrate on using biotechnology to improve the use of Canada's resource base and industrial development.
Microelectronics is also an important area for Canada's technological future. The federal Government will be establishing an initial fund of $7.5 million over two years to support the development of a national microelectronics design network. The funds will help establish a university-based, computer-linked network of design and testing stations for very large scale integrated circuits. About thirty universities are expected to participate in the expanded design network which will be closely integrated with the current work of industry in the microelectronics field. These facilities will help train the manpower critical to the expansion of the Canadian microelectronics industry and make an important contribution toward the creation of a technologically oriented work force for Canada.
Success in all these initiatives depends on the awareness of science and technology on the part of the public.
I am pleased to announce that the federal Government will sponsor a national "Canada Tomorrow" conference in the fall of 1983 which will highlight the effective management of technological change, especially as it affects the working Canadian and industry and trade in this country. This forum will bring the various sectors involved in technology development together-that is, labour, business, universities and Government-to form a deeper understanding of each other's requirements and concerns.
[ Translation]
The provinces also have an important role to play in the technological development of our country. Over the last few years, our activities in this field have increased tremendously. The federal Government intends to work together with the provinces in order to achieve a co-ordinated and harmonious blend of objectives, policies and programs that will launch Canada's recovery.

The Government's commitment to technology is evident, both in the level of current support to research and innovation and in the strong support which the budget has given to research and technology.
The Special Recovery Capital Projects Program has allocated $290 million over the next four years to establish 15 new or expanded research and training facilities. Projects are expected
to substantially expand research capabilities to serve the forest products, fisheries, agri-food, manufacturing and mining industries. In addition, $ 180 million has been allocated for the accelerated procurement of high-technology electronic and communications equipment.
As part of this program I am pleased to inform the House that my colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), has just announced today in St. John's, Newfoundland, the purchase of high technology communications equipment for the Canadian Forces valued at more than $67 million. These purchases include: $19.5 million for the search and rescue satellite project which will provide advanced technology to help locate aircraft and ships in distress; $38 million for a military aeronautical communications system which will be installed at various bases across Canada; $5 million for new high frequency receivers to upgrade the current communications networks; and $5 million for new CW20 microwave communications systems at selected bases across Canada. In addition, the Minister of National Defence announced the allocation of over $20 million to improve helicopter search and rescue capabilities in Canada.
As I said at the outset, over $700 million has been set aside in the budget for technology development. This is in addition to the $3 billion that the federal Government had already budgeted for technology support in the 1983-84 Estimates. It also does not include, and I emphasize this, the $200 million of forgone tax revenues for current R and D expenditures, nor the $185 million the new tax changes and proposals would add to that basic figure.
We must now turn that large and important investment into action. Central to this success is the concerted, co-operative and combined action of all sectors. We now have the policy structure and the fiscal support to push forward Canada's technological advance. It is now up to us to take advantage of the opportunities at hand to build towards a prosperous 1990.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have two questions for the Minister. One of the most recent high technology programs which could be brought in by the Government is the long baseline radio telescope which is proposed for across the country. Does the Minister know if that project is going to go ahead? Second, would its headquarters be at the University of Lethbridge, which I gather from the scientific data is the logical place for that headquarters?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has been no decision taken as yet with respect to the baseline array. Much interest has been expressed in the Hon. Member's own constituency of Lethbridge. I myself, as the Hon. Member may know, have met with representatives of that community, including the President of the University of Lethbridge. Of course, it is a very exciting proposal and a very expensive proposal. It is, indeed, one that deserves close study and that is being done, I understand, by the National Research Council at the present
May 3, 1983

time. However, no decision has been taken with respect to that particular project.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister might comment as to whether he, in his own mind, believes that it is a high technology project and whether it would fit within the 100 projects which the Government has envisaged. However, my second question goes on to another very important research facility in my riding at Lethbridge called the Animal Diseases Research Institute. The Minister knows from his days in the Treasury Board that we have some very top scientists working under very antiquated conditions and in outdated buildings. I am wondering if one of the 100 projects would be new capital spending for the Research Institute in Lethbridge.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member probably knows, I have over-all responsibility for the Special Recovery Capital Projects Program in terms of its moving forward and its co-ordination and implementation. I have said in the past, and would reiterate today for the benefit of Hon. Members of the House, that the specific projects will be announced in the very near future, as they become ready for announcement, by the line Ministers responsible in each case. I would hope that all of the projects will be announced within the next several weeks. I would only ask the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) to bide his time and await those announcements as they are made.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister's colleague about the whole question of plants which just simply close down and move away without any concern for the community or the workers involved, and there are many examples. The Minister speaks about technological changes which must take place and the new technology which must be introduced into Canada. I do not disagree with him for one moment. However, has he addressed the question of what corporate behaviour we could require from those companies which operate here, which receive considerable benefit from our tax structure and which demand in many ways that communities expend tax dollars to create an infrastructure which enables them to operate efficiently and effectively? And how do we demand from them a level of corporate behaviour which requires them at least to sit down with the people most affected, the Governments, the employees, the municipal officials, to discuss their plans in advance and the way in which they might live up to their responsibility to those communities?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would emphasize that, with respect to this whole question of management of technological change, I doubt that there is any area more important and of more concern to the Government, and obviously to the Hon. Member, than the issue of appropriate measures for labour adjustment. That is why there has been proposed the establishment of a national technology productivity centre, whatever the name may ultimately be, to address the very issues which the Hon. Member raises in his question. I am convinced, and I believe members of the community who are very familiar with technological changes as they are taking place across the
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
western world are convinced, that the pace of change and the capacity of our system to take advantage of change in order to improve our productivity would depend very much on the extent to which we address that very issue.
We intend to move forward and do everything we can, Mr. Speaker, to identify the extent of the problem which, as the Hon. Member probably knows, is a subject of some debate- the extent to which these changes will impact on the workplace in the short term and, perhaps more importantly, in the long term. We see short-term impacts, for example, in the clothing, textile and footwear sectors.
As the Hon. Member knows, we have established the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board which has as one of its mandates attempted to address adjustment, to bring new industries into communities affected either through the reduced activity in plants or through the modernization of plants. Because both have their impact on employment levels; there is no doubt about that.
All I would say, Mr. Speaker, is that the question raised by the Hon. Member is very much on our minds and is specifically addressed in the technology policy paper, and will be specifically addressed by my colleagues, the Minister of Labour and the Minister responsible for DRIE, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, as they go forth to try to set the terms and conditions among labour and industry leaders for the establishment and operation of the centre.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister knows, microtechnology, microprocessing and robotronics will be replacing assemblers in many of our industries; in fact, they already have. This is a process which has been going on for a number of years. In fact, Alvin Toffier told us about it five years ago. In view of the fact that it is estimated that some
400,000	assemblers in Canada will be displaced by robotics and microprocessing by 1985, in view of the fact that at the present time there are virtually no facilities for retraining anywhere in Canada which would accommodate a substantial number of employees, and in view of the fact-and I will give a specific example-that in Brantford, Ontario, at Mohawk College, if your Unemployment Insurance benefits have run out, if you are on a retraining program in high-tech, if you are married and have two children, you receive $106 a week to exist on, I would like to know what the Minister and his Department are going to do specifically to address this problem of 400,000 assemblers being displaced by robotronics and microprocessing, with woefully inadequate facilities not only at the present time, but which will continue to be woefully inadequate right down to 1985? What is being done to assist them?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I am not certain that I can verify the number of 400,000, but whatever the number may be it is clear, as I mentioned in my earlier response, that Government, industry, the labour movement itself and the provincial Governments all have to be brought together in a concerted action plan to address the issue of job displacement and retraining.

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
I infer from the Hon. Member's question that he feels that steps which have been taken today have been inadequate. I believe the programs which have been designed and brought forward by my colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) have been very creative and very effective. In fact, I doubt that at any other time in the history of this country, or in the history of many other countries, there has been such ambitious programs brought forward to address the very problem which the Hon. Member raises in his question. I point out that in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance, when dealing with the issue of technology, the Minister said, and I quote from Hansard at page 24667:
Moreover, workers will have to acquire new skills and knowledge throughout their working lives. With this in mind, I am allocating tonight an additional $155 million for human resource development programs. This will bring to $1.2 billion this year the funds allocated for skills development in occupations that are significant for economic growth.
I would suggest, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that indeed the Government has made a very important and major contribution in addressing the very problem which the Hon. Member raises.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) referred in his talk a little earlier to the budget proposals to create industrial incentives for research and development. I would like to ask if these industrial incentives are to take the form of a tax incentive for research and development. This may be applicable to some corporations but there are corporations which may not want, or be in a position to take advantage of, tax incentives. Are there any recommendations which the Minister wants to make in that regard?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is not so much a question of making a recommendation; it is a question of identifying what is being provided. There are special tax investment incentive provisions provided, including the flow out of a tax incentive to new equity purchasers of corporations, which I suggest could be very valuable indeed to some of the firms who are not in a position to take advantage of some of the write-offs which would enable them to acquire effectively more equity.
In addition to that, of course, I referred during the course of my comments to certain specific proposals-

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I really regret to interrupt the Hon. Minister, but the time allotted for questions and comments has expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a lot wrong with this budget. It is a real travesty. It is shortsighted. It looks up to the next election, but it does not look much beyond it. It does not look to the long-term future of the country. Therefore it is irresponsible. It is unfair. It continues the practice of "Those who have, get more", and it is hypocritical. It is full of contradictions throughout. There is the appearance and then there is the reality when you look underneath the appearance and see who actually is going to pay for the programs and is going to benefit from them.

This is not a recovery budget, it is a wait-and-see budget. As an instrument for creating jobs, it is entirely inadequate and powerless. The special recovery program will spend $4.8 billion over the next four years, in other words, an average of $1.2 billion per year. However, if we consider that the Government's monthly bill for unemployment insurance benefits is over $1 billion, the so-called recovery program is certainly not much, compared with this country's unemployment problem. This is wait-and-see, not recovery. We are waiting for the economy to recover elsewhere, especially in the United States, Japan and Europe, and then Canada will resume its traditional role as a supplier of natural resources. The budget mentions programs to encourage research and development in industry, but the proposals it contains will, in our opinion, be totally ineffective. When a problem is not fully understood, the remedy is often useless, due to poor diagnosis. In this case, the Minister has failed to realize that the reason for the lack of research in industry in Canada is the! multinational system. Canadian branch plants and multinationals do not invest in research and development here, because their parent companies do not want them to.
The budget goes on to mention that it is not the fault of Canadian tax incentives, because they are at least as substantial, if not more so, than in other countries. So what does the Government propose to do. Increase tax incentives! There is no mention of the structural reasons for a lack of investment in research and development, and there is no discussion of the real problems. It is a fact that countries like Japan, the United States, Sweden and the Federal Republic of Germany devote a far greater percentage of their gross national product for research and development than we do. Let us consider countries that are financially more independent than we are, where the economy is controlled by that country's citizens, and where companies tend to invest more in research and development than we do with our financial dependent economy, that is controlled from outside by the multinationals. I am afraid that unless we tackle the basic structural problems, we shall not be able to provide the remedies that are required.
There are two parts to this Special Recovery Program; Public Works and Special Recovery Capital Projects. While these may be good in themselves and some projects will certainly be useful, they are generally small projects because it is a pork-barrel budget. These projects are opportunities for Cabinet Ministers to tour the country to announce projects, hold press conferences, turn sod and cut ribbons.
There is no doubt that some needed work will be done; facilities will be built, transportation improved and tourist facilities upgraded. But in certain respects the budget reveals a serious lack of understanding of what is essential, especially
May 3, 1983

with regard to research and development and high technology procurement.
In this respect the budget is drastically in error by what it does not do. It does not begin to ask why we do not conduct adequate research and development in Canada, why we do not export enough and why our enterprises do not have enough incentives to do this. The budget does not address the root causes. However, the budget attempts to be more than just a summary of expenditures and revenue for the next year. There are four-year projects mentioned. There are copious supporting documents. There are projections and analyses, but these are self-serving analyses. No matter how many appendices, tables and graphs are provided to the Minister, they will do very little good if the right questions are not asked.
There are Special Recovery Incentives for Private Investment. This is where the budget moves from a slight touch of Keynesian economics to an enthusiastic endorsement of Reaganomics. The rich have to be bribed with ever more generous gifts to invest their money while low and middle income Canadians are called upon to make sacrifices for national recovery, as in the six and five program or later in the budget when there are tax increases.
This part of the budget is wrong not only because of its inequities, it is misguided. Incentives are provided for businesses to expand but Canadian businesses are working at an average of only 70 per cent capacity. They could be expanding considerably now, a full 30 per cent, without adding any new capacity simply because of under-utilization.
As well, there is the Special Recovery Export Financing Fund. Certainly we are all in favour of stimulating exports, but what this budget proposes is hopelessly inadequate because it does not address the real structural problems inhibiting export in the multinational system. Many branch plants are forbidden to export because they are not to compete with the companies in the parent system.
The Minister is concerned in this program about increasing the deficit and crowding out investment in future years when the recession will presumably be over. Therefore, he has funded it by a special recovery tax. Who is to pay this tax? Consumers are to pay. There is an increase in the manufacturing sales tax from 9 per cent to 10 per cent and a similar increase for construction materials, alcohol and tobacco, although not to be effective until October, 1984 or probably after the next election. An increase in the sales tax is wrong because it certainly is regressive. People with lower incomes pay a higher proportion of their income in sales tax than those with higher incomes. It continues the trend of Liberal Governments to raise taxes mostly from individuals. We will see more evidence of this later in the budget.
The next part of the budget consists of tax giveaways to corporations. Again, we see the trend continued with the manufacturing sales tax where the tax burden on corporations is reduced and increased on individuals. During the 1950s, taxes in Canada were paid roughly half and half between corporations and individuals. Presently, four-fifths are paid by individuals and only one-fifth by corporations.
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
There are changes to the mining depletion allowance, which is already high. It will be made deductible against nonresource income of those who finance mining ventures. While we are all agreed that mining is an important industry, should it be given this much favouritism? Mining has been hard hit not for lack of investment but because of the world recession. It is already highly favoured in taxes compared to other Canadian industries, such as the textile industry, which is an important employer in Canada and pays a much higher proportion of its income in taxes than do mines. Mining provides jobs in the mines and associated services but does not provide manufacturing jobs where there is a better return for the investment dollar in terms of job creation.
Furthermore, Canada imports almost all of its mining machinery and equipment, so that means that we will be providing more jobs for people in other countries, mainly the United States and Europe. Yet we have been given as a reason for not cutting income taxes the fact that Canadians would purchase imported goods. It seems the Minister does not realize that corporations import too, and mining companies import enormously. This is why the NDP has advocated in its industrial strategy the development of a manufacturing sector that could serve our resource industries instead of developing natural resources only. The two should go together; but we see no attempt to move in that direction in this budget.
In housing we see the continuation of the principle that "those who have get more". There is an increase of only 2,500 units planned in the 1980s for social housing. This is an area where we badly need additional housing, certainly in my riding and across the country. But most of the program is devoted to those who can afford to buy a new home.
The demand for more co-ops is often met with the argument that middle-income people are subsidized in co-ops, people who do not need it, yet here we are seeing subsidies of $3,000 in home owner grants to people who can afford a new home. There are provisions in the RHOSP Program, which is a system of tax deductions and as such is an advantage to people who are better off. This plan allows people to withdraw funds for the purchase of furniture and appliances. Certainly we are in favour of stimulating consumption to get people back to work but our concern would be to find efficacious and equitable ways of doing it. Using the tax deduction system to do it is regressive and unfair.
In child benefits, again we see that the appearance and the reality are different. Measures are announced "to provide additional income support for lower income families, working parents and others in need". The child care expense deduction is increased and this, of course, is welcome for the reason that existing provisions were certainly inadequate. But the way the additional relief has been given in objectionable. Tax deductions benefit high earners more than low earners, and people below the taxable income level not at all.
A great commotion was made over continuing the Child Tax Credit, which is advantageous to low and middle income

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Ms. McDonald
earners. It will be continued at the present level when otherwise it would have been dropped. But this is simply giving back what had been taken away. Why was the Child Tax Credit increased? Well, because the Family Allowance was reduced. If the Minister had not reduced Family Allowances in the first place, he would not have had to get into this juggling act of changing funds from source to source.
The Minister is paying for the so-called additional benefits by deindexing the child tax exemption. Since the exemption system is regressive, this is not a bad idea; but a better way would have been to reform fundamentally the whole child support system. It is fraught with inequities and this budget does not address those inequities; it does not come up with a better system, which is what we need. The end result is that people with children will be paying higher taxes in the future, so that this so-called additional income support disappears. The net gain to the Government over the next four years is $585 million from people with children. It is a juggling act. The Minister bounces money from one hand to another, and in the end he ends up with more and families end up with less.
Finally, the budget announces a few innovations which are presumably supposed to make us think the Government is really looking to the future and dealing with basic problems. We are going to have a national centre for productivity and employment growth, and who can be against that? But what confidence do we have that it will even direct the required attention to the real problems? Certainly the budget does not. Is it just going to be another bureaucracy putting out glossy annual reports? Is it going to focus attention on productivity of the worker and not on the structure of industry? Is it going to follow the advice of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), who does not seem to be against importing mining machinery from Sweden or foreign control of our economy, but becomes a positive nationalist when it comes to looking at other countries for their ideas on how to control their own economy. We recommend considering social democratic experiments in Western Europe and looking at the low rates of unemployment. According to him, it is not Canadian to look at social democratic countries in Western Europe, but it is okay to import massively from them and not develop our own economy. If this is the kind of thinking we are going to see at the national centre for productivity and employment growth, we can predict it will not do any good.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, there is a lot wrong with this budget. It is a Conservative budget, full of giveaways to corporations. It is a sly and tricky budget, a pork-barrel, preelection budget. It is unfair. It continues the trend of shifting the burden of taxation on to individuals from corporations. It is shortsighted and does not deal with the real problems of our economy.
The Minister's kerfuffle with the zoom lens has been a boon to the Tories who otherwise would have had very little to criticize in this budget. But to anyone concerned with longterm welfare in this country, it is a pitiful miserable exercise.
I must compliment the Minister for the opportunity he has provided to Cabinet Ministers to pretend something is happening and the clever way he has disguised tax increases in delayed sales taxes and deindexing deductions. But I want to assure him that my Party will do all in its power to expose these sneaky tricks and provide constructive criticism, to outline alternatives, and to direct attention to the real problems undermining our economy and to stress equitable ways of raising taxes so that the burden of running our national economy will be fairly shared. We have an entirely different approach to the budget from what we have seen so far, Mr. Speaker, and we will continue to work for those kinds of alternatives.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I note with interest the comments of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), and I must say that I would agree largely with her general comments regarding the budget. But she referred to the provisions regarding housing, specifically the $3,000 grant to the people who want to buy a house, and then compared that to the minuscule amount provided to co-op housing. Does the Hon. Member know what the subsidy is for co-op housing per unit on the life of the mortgage, since she is casting aspersions on that program?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I could not give a figure and no figure is given in this budget. No amount is given, even for the assistance to co-op housing, simply the number of units; 2,500 units are specified at no particular amount.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, if she will check with CMHC officials, she will understand that this is 2 per cent money we are talking about concerning co-op housing. That is, the Government pay in subsidy form all the money on the mortgage except for 2 per cent which the co-op picks up. When interest rates were highest the subsidy per unit was in the area of $500,000 over the life of a mortgage. Now, with rates lower. I am sure it must be down to about $250,000 or $300,000, which is still a substantial subsidy for those co-ops. It is by no means low-cost housing. It may be low rent housing but not low-cost housing.
I ask her to comment on the relative subsidy comparison between the $3,000 grant for first-time home buyers and a subsidy for co-op housing which could be as high as $300,000 over the life of the mortgage. I then ask her to comment as to whether or not the provisions of CMHC are adequate in making sure that only low-income people live in those co-op housing units, because I can assure her that many middle-class people are taking advantage of that good benefit.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, we have to compare unit by unit. To my knowledge CMHC does not provide the necessary material to do this. Right now co-ops normally have a 25 per cent limit on the number of people at subsidized levels. Many co-ops would be quite happy to go up to 50 per cent but the rules forbid them from doing this, so they would have a much higher proportion of people with low incomes in them. Co-ops certainly in my riding are comprised on average of low-income people but the Member certainly is right, there are some people in the middle income level.
May 3, 1983

I think CMHC should provide data so that comparisons can be made in a careful way. CMHC does not do this. They do not analyse their subsidies by income level at all. There is no ceiling on this and we do not know to what income group the subsidies are actually going. I tried to find out at the time I was housing critic and the information was not available. CMHC had never collected the information. So I am afraid I cannot answer questions when CMHC does not collect the data.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to rise on this occasion to deal with the question before us in the House today, which is the introduction of the new technologies into the structure of Canada's productive machinery; in other words, our economics in Canada.
First, I would like to outline several of the measures that have been taken in the past which bring us to this point in our discussion of the budget today. In 1979 we decided that Canada's performance in terms of research and development was far too low. In 1967 we had reached a level of 1.2 per cent of Gross National Product that was being spent on research and development of the new technologies. From 1967 to 1976 this level of 1.2 per cent of Gross National Product fell to an all-time low of .96 per cent of Gross National Product. In 1978 and 1979 in a responsible fashion we set out to do a great deal about this. We set new, realistic targets. We set a target of 1.5 per cent of Gross National Product by the year 1985 that would be devoted to the new technologies through research and development.
This is not something which the NDP would like perhaps because it is not all being done by the Government alone, but by the Government and the private sector. We felt the major responsibility for creating new research and development in Canada rested with the private sector, that it rested with those firms making the products and having the responsibility for marketing them. Fully one-half of our increased commitment of 1.5 per cent of GNP would have to be satisfied by the private sector. One-third would come from the federal Government and the remaining one-sixth would come from universities, foundations and provincial Governments.
I am very pleased to announce today that we have more than met our targets to date. At the end of 1982 we reached 1.34 per cent of GNP being spent on R and D. I project that we will surpass our 1.5 per cent target by 1985, and I am pleased to announce that both the federal Government and the private sector have exceeded their targets in bringing us to this level.
I must respond to some comments made by the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), primarily because I think she is doing a disservice to the people we are endeavouring to serve and because she is in total conflict with the official Opposition critic of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis).
I want to talk about the $2.4 billion in programs that we are using to generate immediate employment. We have been in favour of infrastructure improvements in order to get jobs
The Budget-Mr. Peterson
going and to accelerate the deployment of capital to bring the jobs onstream now that have been waiting a couple of years on shelves in various areas. These are things that are needed to improve our competitive structure. Perhaps they are institutions which we have to have but which might have been delayed because of the tough economic times we have been facing. We are bringing these forward with $2.4 billion in projects. For the Hon. Member from Broadview-Greenwood to have the audacity to criticize this type of thing-the job creation, the infrastucture improvements and the improvements that will take place in our competitive position because of what we are doing in this area-is, in my view, nothing more than cheap politics.
The Hon. Member from Broadview-Greenwood failed to mention the Special Recovery Program of another $2.4 billion which will be directed over the next three years to help accelerate our recovery from this recession. This includes many incentives for the private sector to help it build up equity bases and to help sell equity capital, to help investors get involved and to increase our exports. What I am particularly proud of is the help this program will give to our industrial infrastructure based on numerous technologies.
Why, I ask in this House, must we always be looking for the cheap shot and why must we always be against something? I have heard some good ideas from Opposition Members in the past. Certainly our capital works project is one project that is agreed to by the official NDP Finance critic. I think when we face serious economic times we should pool our collective expertise, not make cheap political points. We should try to find solutions to the problems that we face.
I would like to comment on what I think are some of the roads that we should be taking in the future so as to increase Canada's productivity and our ability to compete. If we cannot compete internationally, then I am not really sure that we will ever be able to make an economic recovery. We are a trading country. We are dependent upon foreign markets for our produce. But just as important as our raw materials, we are dependent upon foreign markets for the type of manufactured goods that will create jobs in the future. Here again we get into the whole area of high technology.
I believe the public sector and the federal Government have an opportunity to lead in implementing new technologies and in making the public sector more productive. The taxpayers have a right to the best productivity that we can generate. The new technologies, computers, word processors and so on will help us here.
There is a second aspect to the federal Government's role in this area. By using the capacity we have-because we are a huge employer of white collar workers-and by using the federal Government as a laboratory, not only do we improve our own productivity but we can set the lead for the private sector to follow in terms of the new techniques that we can develop which can in turn be passed to the private sector. In other words, we have an opportunity to be leaders in the public

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Peterson
sector in terms of increased productivity by utilizing new technologies.
I was somewhat alarmed to learn the results of a study done by the Ontario Government task force on microtechnology. It indicated certain attitudinal barriers in Canada, that Americans are much more optimistic about what new technologies will do for workers. Canadians, on the other hand, are much more afraid they will be displaced by new technologies and that they will lose their jobs. Americans felt that new technologies will increase their productivity and will make their jobs more interesting. They are far less concerned about displacement.
I want to address that issue particularly because it affects a great number of women in our workplace today. There is a fear that women will be displaced by utilization of new technologies, new machinery and new techniques. To those who are concerned generally and to those who might have concerns arising out of the Ontario Government's task force report, I would refer them to the commission of inquiry into technological change in Australia. That study indicated that there would be an adverse impact on female employment in areas such as telephone operators, bank tellers who are being replaced by the Green Machine, or cashiers being faced with automated cash registers. On the other hand, the study found that there would be incredible opportunities for women in the work force because of the new technologies.
Recent studies conducted in Ontario pointed out that this depended upon the structure of our industry and our business. For example, there are 46,000 charitable organizations in Canada, each of which has at least one female worker. They will not be displaced by new technologies. They can become more productive, more efficient and accomplish a great deal more using the new technologies. They will not be replaced.
Another study indicated that in Ontario the average number of employees in a firm was only four. Almost every one of them employs women. These women will not be replaced by machines which can do things ten times as quickly as the old method. They will have their productivity improved; they will not be replaced. We have to ensure that each new business in Ontariao or, for that matter, throughout Canada has access to the new technologies and knows how to use them.
Approximately 40 per cent of businesses are using updated or newer technologies at present in Canada. This means there is a tremendous market for new machines, new software and new programs. Also this means that many more people have to be trained in how to use them. I am not sure whether this should be strickly the responsibility of the federal Government, as the New Democratic Party implies. It seems to me that the vendors of this equipment who want to have it in the workplace, sell it or lease it, can play that role very adequately. They can train people in the new technologies. This does not mean that the Government does not have a role to play in retraining. Despite the fact that it is not within our constitutional confidence we, the federal Government, by default have
had to make enormous commitments to new training techniques.
I look to a higher level of sophistication and specialization by women in the work force. Their role will not simply be to process data but to interpret it and to make management decisions which are necessary and inexorably flow from the new technologies and data they produce. The education of women is of some concern to me. By 1985 it is predicted that we will need 8,000 engineers and Ph.D. graduates in science and will fall short of that mark by 50 per cent.
The Science Council of Canada has just published an excellent booklet entitled "The Science Education of Women in Canada". It shows that girls in high school 15 years of age and under who drop out of the sciences, physics and maths are doing so at twice the rate of boys. In other words, women are not taking those subjects in high school which will equip them to deal with the new types of technologies which Toffler's "The Third Wave" has brought upon us. This deprives many women of flexibility in career choices. Also it means that in the future we will have fewer women who are capable of assuming management and leadership roles in universities, Governments and industry. We have a duty to bring this type of information to the attention of young people who are at that critical path in their lives when they must determine their career opportunities.
We have a great opportunity in our service sector not to worry about losing jobs but actually about increasing them. "The World Challenge", published by Jean-Jacques Servan-Schreiber, referred to the opportunities that align us, the developed world, by helping to develop the Third World. Not only do we have a moral obligation to see that the Third World becomes industrialized, developed and that its people achieve a higher standard of living, but in so doing there lies tremendous opportunities for Canadians.
I do not want to see our foreign aid budgets cut back, particularly as they apply to Canadian consultants being hired to go abroad and help disseminate these new technologies which will have the possibility of elevating the standard of living of the Third World. In so doing they will also increase the ability of the Third World to buy Canadian technology and services.
Another route at which we should look is one which would take advantage of Canada's unique position in North America and the existing strength of our service sectors. By looking creatively at our system of international tax treaties for the avoidance of double taxation and which deal with withholding taxes, international capital flows and amendments to the Income Tax Act, Canada could become an international financial capital centre, and multinational companies around the world would use Canada as a basis for servicing their capital. They would be taking advantage of our financial institutions, banks, trust companies, loan companies, insurance companies as well as our accountants and legal profession. Money would be coming into Canada which would otherwise have never had an opportunity or a need to come here. This type of approach could vastly increase employment in our
May 3, 1983

service sector and it could put Canada at a crossroads in international capital flows in order to bring Canada even more to the centre of what is our true destiny, that is, a leader in international business and international trade. It could bring our country even more to the forefront of what really is our true future.
I have tried to address what I think are some of the concerns I hear expressed by the electorate of Willowdale and by people who come to see me. The point has been raised by Opposition Members that the new technology is something to fear because it will get rid of jobs. It will require new investment in human capital. It will require individuals themselves to make the effort to learn new ideas and to retrain themselves to cope with the new world they face. I do not look upon this as a threat. It is a challenge and a tremendous opportunity for Canadians to increase their productivity by bringing onstream the new technologies, by working with them, and by using them as our servants in order to increase our standard of living and our ability to compete. We can do it. It is an opportunity that is not a threat. The new technologies are the bit that we will use to drill our way into a new world of international competitiveness based upon exports, long production runs, manufacturing, and a much greater use of the new technologies.
I am pleased that the thrust of the new technologies is one of the linchpins of our new budget. It is one of the reasons the budget was so well received by Canadians from all walks of life.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not very often congratulate a Member of the Government on his comments, but the Hon. Member's speech was very constructive. It was a good speech. I agree with him about the importance of research and development and to make public corporations and the various levels of Government aware of that importance.
I have one or two questions I would like to put to the Hon. Member. He indicated that the Government had met its target as far as expenditures on research and development are concerned. He gave a figure of 1.5 per cent of the Gross National Product. Could he indicate the Government's target for research and development in agriculture and whether he feels that target has been met?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be pleased to obtain that information. I do not have the figures on the specific breakdown. I know that we have taken a lead in terms of the new installations in Saskatchewan in dealing with hydrology and the very important impact that has on agricultural producers. You cannot produce crops in Saskatchewan without having a very good reading of the types of soil conditions and particularly the water content.
I am proud to say that Canada has been a leader in the area of agriculture. Our agricultural sector deserves a tremendous compliment. The Holstein cow, for example, is regarded throughout the world as probably the best giver of milk. With the new open transplants and the ability to preserve and ship
The Budget-Mr. Peterson
semen around the world, Canadian cows are probably in almost every country of the world that is a milk producer.
We have in the past developed the single best type of wheat, No. 1 Northern. This has required a great deal of innovation, research and development. It does not mean that we have achieved everything we want to in the realm of agriculture, but the agricultural technology developed in Canada is probably without parallel in the world.
Part of our CIDA program involves disseminating this new technology for agriculture around the world. The Hon. Member makes a very valid point. There is probably as much value added in science and technology that goes into producing that kernel of wheat which is now a world leader in export markets as in some of our newer manufacturing plants.
If the Hon. Member's point is that we are going to neglect our traditional industries as they may not appear to have high-tech involved in them, it is a misunderstanding and I hope Members on all sides of the House will address and deal with that directly.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no question that the research that has been done by the Department of Agriculture over the years is some of the finest in the world. Unfortunately, however, if one examines the Estimates over the past number of years, one will note that the increase in the budget for research and development in agriculture is about 1 per cent. It has fallen far behind the rate of inflation in this country. This is unfortunate, because if we are to increase our production of grain and other crops, we must not only keep up to date but keep ahead of other countries as far as research and development is concerned. If nothing else, I hope that the Hon. Member will impress upon the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) the importance of research and development in agriculture, not only by the Government but by the private sector.
It is rather unfortunate that it took the Minister of Agriculture a number of years to release some $9 million of prairie farm assistance money to an organization in the prairies interested in research and development. The matter has been discussed for several years. Only today a news release came across my desk showing that some $9 million had been turned over to this organization from the old PFRA fund, $9 million of farmers' money that had been held since 1972, non-interest bearing. If that money had been turned over years ago for research and development, just think of the progress that could have been made in the private sector in co-operation with the public sector.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not familiar with the particular issue raised by the Hon. Member but I will certainly be pleased to look into it. The point he makes about the necessity for continually re-evaluating what we are doing in the field of agriculture is critical. I look at opportunities which Canadian consumers have to save money and to buy Canadian. Why do people necessarily have to purchase fresh fruit and vegetables from abroad during our winter months? During our summer months we can grow more than enough to feed all

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Peterson
Canadians, if we are prepared to put it into cans. With a little research and development, possibly using solar energy or the new types of energy which we have in abundance, we can grow fresh fruits and vegetables all winter at very little cost, maybe even at a saving compared to the cost of imports.
This goes back to one of my other pet projects in this area. Why are Canadian consumers not more aware of the tremendous opportunities we have to exercise the sovereignty of our buying dollar when we go into the stores to "Buy Canadian"? Why do they not look for the "Made in Canada" label? I would venture to say that in the stores you can find comparable quality at a comparable price for Canadian-made goods. Even if you have to pay a couple of pennies more because other countries have an advantage in certain areas, why do Canadians not exercise their right as consumers to help their fellow producers?
Why do all Canadians not engage in a mutual self-help exercise? The agricultural area is a perfect place to start looking at this. This is something we can do every week when we visit the shopping market. Another point which the Hon. Member makes-

speechtext: Order. Under the procedure, a Member should not abuse the time for questions and replies. The point has been replied to and another Member is seeking the floor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very interested in and totally in agreement with the statement of the Hon. Member regarding self-sufficiency in food and more production of food in Canada. The Hon. Member has a little more influence in Government than we do. Would he actively support a job-creation program and economic development project that would encourage and give assistance to the development of food producer co-operatives and consumer food co-operatives? If every community could have solar greenhouses which were operated co-operatively, with start-up funds from the Government, this could be greatly expanded. Would the Hon. Member consider this special project and work within his Party and Government to that end?
