speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yes, I certainly see the co-op movement as one which has taken off on its own without the necessity of Government intervention, because enterprising individuals feel that they can derive benefits by working together. They do not need the heavy hand of Government to legislate or fund them. There are many co-ops that have established themselves without Government support. I have a great deal of respect for many of the co-ops I have seen. We see co-ops in financial institutions, we see them in many small towns in rural Ontario, we see huge co-ops that work very effectively in the west. If enabling legislation and the removal of some red tape impediments is all that is necessary, fine. I want to consider the question of how much public funding
must go into these co-ops, since they have already demonstrated in many areas that they can produce dividends without the necessity of dipping into the taxpayers' pockets in order to make them feasible.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and take part in this debate today. It is indeed a very important debate on a very important budget. In many regards this budget is like no other budget we have had. I realize that there is to be a vote on the budget. There was a vote last Thursday, one that was remarkably close. Only 15 votes separated the two sides. Unfortunately, the NDP was otherwise engaged, 12 of their Members being absent for the vote. This prevented the difference from being narrowed down to three votes. One must realize that 12 Members, nearly 40 per cent of the NDP's strength, were away; it is 37.5 per cent, I believe. We have grown to expect that when the Liberal Government is in danger, the NDP will rush to their rescue, whether it means rushing away from the House or rushing into it.
This budget has a deficit of a size that is astonishing to the world, I suppose. I was listening to the radio this morning and heard that there is concern that the American deficit is not being looked after by the United States Government. If the United States Government does not do something about the size of its deficit, it will have a dramatic effect on the markets in the world.
On a per capita basis, their deficit is about two-thirds of that of Canada. In other words, our deficit is about 50 per cent higher per person than that of the United States. The deficit in the United States is causing some concern throughout the world, though their deficit is relatively modest compared to ours.
The budget has created this enormous deficit of $31.4 billion. We seem now to have the worst of all possible worlds. It is bad that the deficit is extraordinarily high, but this can usually be excused on the basis that it will create jobs. However, reading the figures of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) on the job situation and when he expects the unemployment rate to ease off, it is not apparent that the unemployment rate will ease off in the future. We have both worlds at their very worst; high unemployment and a high deficit running side by side into the future.
In the past, budget speeches and Throne Speeches provided an opportunity for Members with special interests to present speeches that were not necessarily relevant to either the budget speech or the Throne Speech. Things are getting worse these years. As Mr. Speaker will well remember, it has been so long since we have had a Throne Speech that I am not certain that anybody will remember how we deported ourselves. It seems to me that the last Throne Speech in recent memory was way back several years ago. At that time, Members had the opportunity to speak during those speeches. New Members of the House could make mainden speeches on any subject they chose. I must say that I miss the free and easy-going debates of those days. I would highly recommend to the Government that
May 3, 1983

it screw up its courage and try to have one more Throne Speech while it is still in power.
The budget debate to date has been extremely interesting. There have been some remarkably good speeches. We have just heard a couple of speeches that I thought were of outstanding quality. While I disagree with almost everything the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) said, I believe her words accurately represent her feelings. We have just heard a good speech on the budget from the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Peterson) as well. I feel it is a pity that the Minister of Finance never gets to hear any budget speech but his own. We listened to his speech and 1 feel he should return the compliment once in a while and appear in the House to hear what the rest of us, including some Members of his own Party, think of his budget.
I would like to speak about the effect the budget and the fiscal policy of the Government might have on the defences of this country. The projected budget of the Department of National Defence looks fairly good on paper, but it is based upon a faulty premise. For many, many years the Department of National Defence has operated according to its own inflation model. That is, calculations were conducted every few months to indicate what the inflation rate would be over the next few years.
As the years go by, the Department of National Defence has become a very large user of high technology equipment and materials. The Department of National Defence has more expenses and a higher inflation rate than any other Department. Consequently, because of the inflation model that is followed, the DND index would likely show an inflation factor of 15 per cent when the CPI was running at, say, 12 per cent. Treasury Board accepted this rate and would use it in its calculations to give the Department of National Defence an increase in real terms, as it is known. Treasury Board would add in the 15 per cent plus 3 per cent if it was hoping for a 3 per cent increase.
The Department of National Defence must now take a different tack. The Minister of Finance, presumably with the concurrence of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), has decided that this is too good for DND so he will force it to use the Department of Finance's model to calculate the inflation rate starting next year. This will result in an entirely false figure for an increase in real terms based on a inflation rate that will be considerably lower than the actual inflation rate on the commodities that Defence must buy, particularly if it is reequipping itself.
The Department of National Defence certainly needs an increase in purchasing power in real terms because, particularly in the early years of what have come to be known as the Trudeau years, the Government was so determined to wither the Department of National Defence and reduce it in size that it froze the budget in an inflationary cycle and consequently the Department had a bitter choice to make. It was thought that this choice would only affect the Department for one year, perhaps 1969 or 1970. The Department decided that it would hold on to its strength in manpower and cease to maintain
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
buildings and buy equipment, believing that the following year, as it had been assured, things would be back to normal. Well, things did not get back to normal for three or four years, and by the end of that time not only was DND without replacement equipment for those four years, but in addition it finally had to cut its manpowers strength, and down it went to its present level.
The Department of National Defence sunk so low that at one time its capital budget represented only 9 per cent of its total budget. This is really a shocking figure because in this modern world between 25 per cent and 30 per cent of the defence budget must be spent on capital equipment such as tanks, ships and planes to maintain a modern, capable force that can accomplish the tasks that one would expect of one's national defence forces. In the forecast of the Minister of Finance, between the 1981-82 budget and the 1985-86 budget spending will suddenly be cut by $392 million on top of the other cuts.
The budget produced in June, 1982 by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), when he was Finance Minister, as a kind of last gasp effort to do a job of which he was incapable, cut $200 million off the DND budget, to be spread over the next two years. The present Minister cut a further $230 million as a kind of rival gift, to be spread over 1983-84 and 1984-85. When making the cuts at that time the Minister of Finance noted that they would "require some adjustment in the nature of the programs we had planned to undertake". How much more adjusting can we expect the Department of National Defence to make?
We then have the rather ridiculous scene of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) at a conference of defence associations pointing out that DND is due to receive $20 million for "increased readiness and sustainability". This could take the form of ammunition, equipment, spares or even personnel and could involve either the regular or reserve forces. When compared with the $430 million that has been taken from the Department within a year, it can be seen that this leaves quite a deficit. Even with the current budget which allocates $75 million to DND, it is still down $335 million. This is not going to make a difficult cash flow situation for equipment programs any easier.
I should like to say a few words about employment programs that are being discussed these days, Mr. Speaker. DND is supposed to receive $60 million this year and $15 million next year for the Extended Youth Training and Employment Program. Under this program 5,000 people are to be trained and paid the same as recruits in the regular force, but they will officially be Class C reservists with no pension or benefits. They can be had a little cheaper that way. DND officials have been quoted as saying they were as surprised as I was at the low 5,000 figure, as they had expected as many as 20,000.
What will happen to these 5,000 people when their training is completed? Why will the Government not build on this

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon
program and make use of the young people who have one year's training? That would be an ideal time to increase the manpower ceiling for the regular forces and to make use of the people who have already gone through an extensive part of their training. It would give them the opportunity of staying on after the employment program ends.
In the last few days we have heard of a conflict between the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), who has been trumpeting his great NEED Program over the land. The purpose of this program is to employ on a short-term basis people who have exhausted their Unemployment Insurance benefits. The Department of National Defence is to be one of the beneficiaries of this. But it must have work that needs to be done, so it simply fired term employees to make room for NEED employees. Many of these term employees have worked for the Department for years. After a fixed term they must be rehired if they are to continue working there. It is an "in" joke in the Department that the term ends on March 31 and on April 1 these people are rehired. In the last five years only 15 term employees have been discharged and that includes, as far as we can discover, 14 who went out on pension.
The two Ministers seem to be working a double shuffle using a revolving-door principle. They have let hundreds go from what those people had considered to be fairly permanent jobs and they apparently intend to hire people who have exhausted their Unemployment Insurance benefits. A year from now the process can be reversed: they can rehire those who were let go last month and let the people go who were hired this month. The result simply is a doubling of the cost of the work being done.
I should like to move on to the capital programs now and concentrate on the navy because I worry more about the naval equipment program than about anything else when it comes to re-equipping the forces at the present time. The Leopard program to supply the army with a certain number of tanks has pretty well been completed. The CF-18 program is moving along to help the air force. Unfortunately, the equipment for the navy is so long in production that I believe politicians do not like to support it as they are not likely to see the finished product within three elections or so. That makes it difficult for politicians to give the program the support they should.
A year and a half ago the Minister of National Defence, speaking to the Conference of Defence Associations, issued a press release saying that we needed five more Gate vessels to replace the old ones that had been in service for years. Strangely enough, this item disappeared from the Estimates this year. When we asked about them we were told that they were still somewhere but were not a high priority, despite the fact that when the Minister announced them with some fanfare a year ago last January they had a very high priority. Now they have just disappeared.
There is a long list of naval equipment programs, Mr. Speaker. In the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence Committee on March 17 this year I asked for a list of programs but I have not received it. There are many major equipment programs that have not been approved
by Cabinet. The Canadian patrol frigate program will run into billions of dollars, but only $60 million has ever been approved by Treasury Board. The Minister has turned over to Cabinet the decision as to which of two consortia will build the patrol frigates. We are very concerned about the rumours we hear from the Treasury benches-"skid row" as it is otherwise known-about the possibility of that choice being made for political reasons rather than on the basis of the best plan for the best ship. I hope the fact that Scan Marine is totally surrounded by Liberal constituencies will not direct the contract to the wrong consortium simply for political reasons.
While I am on the subject of the Canadian patrol frigates, Mr. Speaker, I might say that there is no way any shipyard in Canada can find the skilled personnel needed to complete the program. If one shipyard were to get the order for the six frigates, there is no way it could build them within the time frame that has been set out. There are not that many technicians who are able to work in any of the existing shipyards in one location. This Party had suggested-although we do not demand author's rights-that it might be a very good idea to build two ships in the Maritimes, two in the St. Lawrence valley and two on the West Coast. That would help not only to maintain a withering industry but to revitalize it. We do have the skills in our people to be able to carry out this kind of work, and I hope that when the Government makes the decision, first, it will not be on political grounds and, second, it will be one that will spread the benefits across this country the way they should be, and not concentrated where the Party which is temporarily in power has a greater strength.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I would like to compliment the previous speakers on their presentations in this important debate and I look forward to any questions they might have.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know the Hon. Member speaks out of a wealth of experience. The one area he did not touch on, however, in the budget had to do with the recruitment program for cadet training and, I suppose, in other jocular terms, getting young people involved in the Armed Forces for a one-year training program. Would the Hon. Member comment on the budget provision in that area in terms of the number of people it would affect and how prepared the Armed Forces are to help?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, General Withers, the Chief of Defence Staff, pointed out not too long ago that they would not be able to train people with their present budget. If they had a sudden requirement for training large numbers, they simply would not be able to provide it. This is a situation which would get much worse if there was an emergency where they would not only have to provide for any reinforcements, but it would take their most experienced people away from their regular units. There is a terrible shortage in that particular area.
May 3, 1983

As far as cadet training is concerned, there is really nothing more important. There is no particular area of the force which is more important than cadet training. We did have some wonderful cadet training camps but they have been starved for funds over the years. That seems to be one of the places, unfortunately, which the Government has restricted far more than it should have over the last few years. Consequently, all kinds of cadets who wish to go to summer camps are not able to do so because of lack of funds.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a further question regarding the frigate program which the Hon. Member mentioned. Does he see any movement on the part of the Government to do any of this construction in the Vancouver-Victoria area?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the fact that that would make an awful lot of sense does not mean that the Government is going to do it. As I said earlier, there is no shipyard anywhere in the country which could take on the job of building six frigates and finish them in the time frame which has been laid down for the ships to be ready. As everyone knows who has studied the situation, by 1991 we are going to have a ten-ship navy at the rate we are going. If they were to put those six frigates into one shipyard to be constructed, it would be 1993 before we get back up to a ten-ship navy, which is generally not thought to be satisfactory to any Canadian.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question to the Hon. Member is with respect to the Cruise missile, the discussions which have gone on and the confrontations about the possibility of having Canada provide air space for the plan to test the guidance system of the Cruise missile. Has the Hon. Member and his Party taken an official position on whether or not this is desirable?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the position of the Conservative Party of Canada that we should encourage, and our Government should encourage, the superpowers to negotiate at the disarmement table in Geneva in order to make enough progress towards restricting and controlling nuclear weapons in Europe that it would not be necessary to deploy the Pershing II or the Cruise missile in Europe. These talks are going on. President Reagan has made a major concession in that he no longer insists on the zero-zero option which seemed to be the main stumbling block at the time. He has given ground on that. I hope that the U.S.S.R. would make a counter offer at this time.
If all else fails, if these negotiations are non-productive, then NATO is going to have to go ahead with the commitment it made in 1979 to the West European nations that it would deploy the Cruise missile and the Pershing II. If it comes to that-and that will be the last resort-then this Party will not complain about the Government authorizing the testing of the Cruise missile at Cold Lake.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would assume from that answer, then, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Member and his Party accept the logic of the NATO two-track proposition.
The Budget-Mr. McKinnon

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hesitate to point out to the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, that this Party was in power when the two-track system was adopted.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That has not prevented the Conservative Party, Mr. Speaker, now that they have moved to the Opposition, from changing their policy on other things. Therefore I wanted to ensure that at least in this policy the Conservative Party has continued to carry on a one-track policy.
My second question for the Hon. Member concerns the testing of the Cruise in Canada, particularly guidance systems. As I understand the purpose of the testing of the Cruise in Canada, it is not necessarily to test the guidance system which would be used in a European context, but rather to test the guidance system which would be useful in a North American context as well; in other words, a more elaborate testing of guidance systems as they have developed.
In the event that the two-track policy fails, that there is an unwillingness or inability to come to an accommodation, would the Hon. Member then be prepared to proceed with the testing of the Cruise missile for North American purposes as opposed to testing the Cruise missile guidance system for European purposes?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a great deal made by uninformed people about this testing of one type of missile when there is a different kind going to be deployed in Western Europe. If we were to test the Cruise missile, that is, air launched, in Cold Lake, if it comes to that, and if the Government decides to go ahead with it-it has kept its option open- the purpose of the test is to test the guidance system and it is identical in both of these otherwise not similar weapons. They are both Cruise missiles, but there are two kinds. One is made by one company and one is made by another. They are both going to use exactly the same guidance system, and that is the connecting link. It really makes no difference. It simply is cheaper in one way to launch it from the air in order to carry out the guidance system test, which is what my understanding is of what is going to be tested at Cold Lake, if indeed any tests are going to be conducted at Cold Lake.

subsubtopic: ADJUDICATION OF FRIGATE CONSTRUCTION CONTRACT-BENEFITS FOR QUEBEC
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the final adjudication of the frigate construction contract for the Department of National Defence is approaching. The Minister repeated not long ago that he was expecting a final decision before the House adjourns for the summer. In its April 30 issue, the Financial Post gave an analysis of the situation and indicated quite clearly that National Defence officials tended to favour the offer made by the consortium located in St. John.
Madam Speaker, in a speech I made not long ago on the subject, I indicated that Quebec shipyards have demonstrated their leadership in the Canadian shipbuilding industry. The decision to be made by departmental officials and Cabinet will, of course, be based on considerations of a technical and qualitative nature. However, they will also have to consider, first of all, the extent of the benefits to Quebec, and second, the quality of the workmanship involved, and third, the considerable technological advantage to our province if a Quebec shipyard is awarded what appears to be the contract of the century.
Speaking on behalf of the riding of Levis, I am counting on a decision that will be based on all of these considerations.


NATIONAL REVENUE	-

Madam Speaker, I would like to address a problem that a small business in my constituency is experiencing with Revenue Canada. A machinery dealer called Layton Green Incorporated, which operates out of Albany, P.E.I., has been fined by Revenue Canada for sending its taxation remittance forms in late for the months of January and February, 1983.
The taxation remittance forms, which are a record of paid deductions, in the form of Canada Pension Plan, unemployment insurance and income tax, which are deducted for the employees' salaries, must be sent to Revenue Canada in St. John's, Newfoundland, by the tenth of the following month. Layton Green Incorporated has, on occasion, not received these forms until on or past the due date. Therefore it is unable to have these forms mailed to St. John's on time. The firm is prompt in completing the forms and mailing them once they are received, but cannot help the fact that it does not receive the forms in time to meet the due date. It has been unjustly fined a percentage of what was listed in the taxation remittance forms for January and February, 1983.
I urge that Revenue Canada ensure that its taxation remittance forms are mailed in time to allow businesses to send them back before the tenth of the following month and not expect businesses to pay fines for a delay which Revenue Canada or Canada Post has caused.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S CONCERN FOR PEACE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the statements made by the New Democratic Party and groups of citizens concerned for peace, I would like to state in this House that I will march and work with pacifist movements when they demonstrate for disarmament in front of Communist countries' embassies as often and as strongly as they do in front of the Parliament buildings. As an elected Member of this House, it is my duty to preserve the fundamental values recognized by the Canadian Parliament, such as the freedom of speech. That is why I urge all Canadians concerned for world peace to denounce the presence of Soviet weapons and military advisors in Cuba if American assistance to El Salvador is to stop. I also urge them to protest against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan, the Soviet repression in Poland against union members and the Polish people, the installation of Soviet missiles in Syria and the presence of 330 SS-20 missiles with three war heads all aimed at European capitals.
Madam Speaker, the freedom we enjoy in our democratic countries cannot be based on the naivety of unilateral pacifists. Working for peace is part of our duty as Canadian parliamentarians. That is why I would like all Members of this House to reflect seriously on the consequences of an intervention not intended to result in a controllable bilateral disarmament. Canada must continue to support this option which is the only valid one, so as to safeguard the freedom of all Canadian men and women.

subsubtopic: FEE CHARGED FOR LIGHT AIRCRAFT RADIO LICENCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last year a radio licence for a light aircraft was increased to $40 and representations were made to the Department and to the Minister, and it appeared that the price would be reduced in 1983. It has not been reduced, and again farmers and businessmen who operate light aircraft are being charged $40 for a licence for the radios in their aircraft while Canadian registered ocean liners, the largest ships afloat, operating out of Canadian ports, only pay $20 per annum.
May 3, 1983

In the United States there is no fee at all for licences for radios in aircraft because the Americans recognize that the radio is not an entertainment item but a safety item. The Canadian Government requires the radio, and then charges an excessive fee for the licence. These same farmers and businessmen are asked to apply the six and five restraint program to their operations, but the Government sticks them with this enormous increase.
I strongly urge the Minister to roll back this fee or, alternately, make it the fee for a five-year period or, better still, wipe it out altogether, as radio is an integral part of the aircraft. Will carburetors be licensed next? Surely the Government and the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) know that the private aircraft industry already contributes substantial sums of money to the federal Treasury through taxes collected for fuel, and also provides jobs. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) is pleading with the private sector to co-operate. Here is an opportunity for the Government to show that co-operation is a two way street.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC RELATIONS EXERCISE-CONDEMNATION OF MAGAZINE ARTICLE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today in The Globe and Mail we read how a bank magazine is telling bankers how to close down plants successfully, keep information away from Opposition MPs, manipulate the press, and hold press conferences away from the affected plants so the workers cannot respond. At a time when Bishops in Canada have talked about economic morality, it is disgusting and typical to see banks looking at PR techniques which are not concerned about the workers or the people who are suffering through foreclosures.
Madam Speaker, I call on the Canadian Bankers Association, which owns the magazine, to disavow that statement, to disavow any claim of authorship for the remarks made in that article. Canadians are suspicious of banks at a time when houses and farms are being foreclosed, but if they are going to allow that kind of article to stand it will be just another nail in the coffin of the Canadian banking system.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: NECESSITY TO AMEND MATERNITY BENEFIT PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Last Friday, Madam Speaker, I was very interested and almost delighted to read the statement of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James (Mr. Keeper) concerning amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act with respect to maternity
benefits. The night before, during a committee meeting, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) stated that he was prepared to introduce amendments with a view to including maternity benefits and other changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act if the New Democratic Party would agree to adopt that Bill quickly so as to enable the Government to implement those changes, keeping in mind the heavy work load of Parliament.
After that conciliatory offer by the Minister, Madam Speaker, we have yet to hear from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-St. James whether his party would be prepared to agree to such amendments, and especially to give unanimous consent so that the Bill might be adopted as quickly as possible. Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is posing as the defender of women's interests throughout the country, so he should now give us a clear and final answer to pave the way for that Bill including those amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subsubtopic: NECESSITY FOR RESEARCH FUNDING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, research and development are the essence of progress in any society. This truism, however, receives hardly any recognition in our country where research, and agricultural research in particular, are given second priority. As a result the challenges offered by developing new varieties and new crops and more productive ways of farming can be lost to us forever. This, in turn, will hamper Canada's future capability to catch up with increasingly competitive international markets and to meet the targets set up by our agri-food strategists.
It is essential that our researchers start now to build the foundations for research in subjects like genetic engineering, improved energy efficiency, and waste utilization.
Researchers and scientists have expressed their concern about the curtailment of research funding and the shortage of qualified staff. Yet Cabinet appears to turn a deaf ear to all the criticism and continues to defend cutbacks in research staff so badly needed and so short in supply.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is obviously aware of the publication by his own Department "Challenge for Growth-an Agri-food Strategy for Canada". The authors of the publication do not share the Minister's contentment with the status quo in our research, and point out losses in Canadian agriculture due to the inadequate support of research.
May I suggest that the Minister have a closer look at this document and familiarize himself with the lost opportunities.

May 3, 1983

subsubtopic: CROWSNEST PASS RATE-SUPPORT FOR RETENTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the House to the misrepresentations being made by the Minister of Transport concerning Crow rate retention. The Minister told the House on Friday that retention is the position of only the New Democratic Party and the National Farmers Union. That is not so. Crow retention is also the position of a majority of grain producers and people of the West.
I can demonstrate this quite easily by referring to my own Prince Albert region, which is a typical grain growing area. To date I have received one single letter backing the Pepin proposal for Crow change. For Crow retention, I have tabled 3,500 signatures on petitions in the House and I have 2,000 individual endorsements of retention. I have also received specific letters backing retention from 23 towns, villages, and rural councils. They include the communities of Hudson Bay, Choiceland, Canwood, Marcelin, Rosthern, Carrot River and Shell Lake. The same support came from the rural municipalities of Kinistino, Spiritwood, Garden River, Kelvington, Ponass Lake, Arborfield, Buckland, Torch River, Willow Creek, Blaine Lake, Fleet's Springs, Canwood and Birch Hills.
The Council and Chamber of Commerce of the City of Prince Albert have also supported retention. This is support from one small segment of the Province of Saskatchewan. The essence of democracy is having the consent of the governed. The Minister has ignored that essence.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was with utter disbelief that I watched a report carried on the CBC Journal last night concerning the firing of an Alberta teacher, Mr. Keeg-stra, who had been teaching anti-Semitic trash to his students for over 14 years.
In an interview Mr. Keegstra confirmed his belief that Jewish conspirators had caused the French Revolution, the U.S. Civil War, the assasination of Lincoln, and he also trotted out the ridiculous allegation that the Jews had started the First and Second World Wars.
He went on to defend some of the ideas of Adolf Hitler, and even questioned whether the Holocaust had, in fact, occurred. He challenged the interviewer to produce the evidence.
What shocked and horrified me, and I speak as one who visited the Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem last month, was that, notwithstanding his own admission that he had been teaching his students this garbage, numerous school officials, including his principal, schoolboard officials, fellow teachers and officials of the Teacher's Association, had continued to defend his right for some time to continue teaching, on the assumption that it would stimulate discussion. As a Canadian and a Christian I was stunned to learn of this seeming indifference of responsible people in our school system to such blatant racism. Hopefully, we will all learn something from this sad episode, namely, that we must be ever vigilant to prevent the ugly seeds of racism in any form, including anti-Semitism, from poisoning the schoolchildren and the minds of our youth.
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: DEFINITION OF HANDICAPPED PERSON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, National Revenue has an interpretation bulletin number IT-225 which defines a handicapped person for income tax purposes. For its purposes, a handicapped person is one who is confined to a bed or wheelchair for more than 12 hours a day, a substantial part of the day or night. That is a definition not designed to help the handicapped but to help income tax officials make easy decisions in classifying people.
Some three and a half years ago this House unanimously passed a resolution during Private Member's Hour asking Finance officials to redefine that particular bulletin and change the definition of a handicapped person for income tax purposes. That still has to be done.
I note with interest that in the last budget presented by the Minister of Finance he has graciously doubled the deduction allowed to parents for educational purposes of their children because he wants to help comfortable, middle-class parents. Meanwhile, those parents who want to assume the responsibility for the training of their children who happen to be handicapped are left out and not taken care of.
It is time that the officials of the Tax Department of National Revenue took their responsibility seriously and looked beyond the pretty "obstacles" report which does not require the Government to do anything. It seems to me that the goal of this Government is to do all things that are pretty but that do not obligate it to spend any money.
May 3, 1983

This money was under the control of the Government of Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: CAPE BRETON COAL AGREEMENT-CONTRACT BETWEEN GOVERNMENT AND GERMAN FIRM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was not aware of that contract, but I have checked the record today. Indeed, there was a contract with that company which was signed in January.
As the Hon. Member should know, there are about 20 liquefaction projects that have been studied over a long period of time with the help of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.

May 3, 1983

I want to give some examples. Two Opposition Members who spoke yesterday in this House indeed indicated previously their approbation of the budget. I draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the Midland Free Press in which the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) described the budget thus:
The MP said Tuesday he was pleased with the Government's plan to expand the mandate of the Federal Business Development Bank. The FBDB will provide greater support for small business and include a new investment banking capability to help meet the capital needs of promising small companies.
"That's what small business is looking for," said Lewis.
The MP also was pleased with the phasing out of the standard $100 tax deduction claimed in lieu of itemized deductions for charitable donations and medical expenses.
The lifting of existing limits on investment tax credits is "healthy," said Lewis, the Conservative House Leader.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that with that sort of endorsement we will see the Opposition House Leader vote with the Liberal Party and the Government on the occasion of the final adoption of this measure. I call your attention as well to the Enterpriser Bulletin of Collingwood, Ontario, where the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) is quoted as follows:
Grey-Simcoe MP Dr. Gus Mitges said the special projects should help the unemployment situation.
"A lot of the budget is pointed in that direction," he said.
"You've got some good things for farmers and the doubling of the child care deduction is a good thing," he said.
I say again that I invite that Hon. gentleman, when the time comes for the vote, to vote in favour of the budget and join the Government Party in so doing.
The last Member I would like to quote is the new Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall), which is just north of my particular region. He is quoted as follows:
For Mr. MacDougall, the budget did contain some good news. He cited the one month extension of the $3,000 federal grant to new home buyers, to the end of May, 1983. He also praised the Home Ownership Savings Program referred to in the budget.
While he approved of the investment tax incentives introduced by the Finance Minister-
That shows the high level of excellence of this particular document and the amount of approbation it is receiving throughout the whole of the community.
I would also like to indicate what happened on the street the day after the budget was brought down. The Toronto Stock Exchange rose by 43.75 points, the most impressive postbudget rise since records have been kept at the Toronto Stock Exchange. The dollar went up two-fifths of a cent as a result of this budget. Indeed, Wall Street indicated that it praised the budget for its philosophy and structure. For Wall Street to have indicated approbation of this budget based upon economic philosophy and structure, Madam Speaker, is really a welcome development.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. If the Hon. Member was addressing his remarks to the Chair, he would notice that I am not wearing robes or a skirt!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
The Budget-Mr. Blais

I apologize, Mr. Speaker. Of course, the other problem is that I would like to speak to the issue of capital projects because, as it has been pointed out, over $1 billion will be allocated through procurement.

Indeed, when the $2.4 billion was approved in the budget for capital projects I was most pleased, because of that amount over $1 billion will be invested through procurement. As you know, Mr. Speaker, my Department is very interested in showing its colours in terms of effective negotiation of contracts. Comments have been made by Opposition Members to the effect that indeed there might be some difficulties through the allocation process where there may be some favouritism manifested. I want the House to rest assured, Mr. Speaker, that the total operation will be in accordance with the contract regulations and the Financial Administration Act, and it is our responsibility and the responsibility of this House so to ensure.
There is going to be fast-tracking-and I think the word is well chosen-of the operation within my Department because preliminary approval of the projects is granted immediately by a subcommittee of the Priorities and Planning Committee. I sit on that subcommittee, Mr. Speaker, and I can assure you that the process is being followed very expeditiously and that most of the projects have already received approval.
The other way in which fast-tracking is accomplished is through increased contract delegation to individual Departments, which means that we can go into the marketplace and through the tendering process negotiate contracts for higher amounts without having to submit the application to Treasury Board for approval. That is one way of fast-tracking. The other way is by setting up a special recovery projects board which involves Deputy Ministers who will ensure that all of the bureaucratic impediments are removed in order to accelerate the process. Again, I spoke of the approval process which has been delegated to a subcommittee of Ministers of the Priorities and Planning Committee.
You will recall that we made the claim that we would reduce the approval time from the time the requirement was identified to the time the work was put in place by 50 per cent. That is exactly our intention and it is exactly what we will do. We are killing two birds with one stone, Mr. Speaker. First of all we are creating jobs, there is no doubt about that. The second point is that we are putting in place a highly desirable infrastructure, and we are procuring goods required by the Government of Canada and its agencies. I would like to quote from the Minister's budget speech. He said:
The projects will focus on six key areas; transportation, research and training facilities, resource development, vessel procurement, land and tourism development and high technology procurement. The projects are future-oriented, aiming to build and upgrade research and high technology centres, transportation infrastructure and other facilities and services that will enhance the long-term growth potential of Canadian industry. They will provide much needed support for several currently weak sectors of the economy, such as construction, shipbuilding, Fisheries and forestry.
May 3, 1983

The Budget-Mr. Blais
Hon. Members will recall that we announced two of those major projects on Monday of last week. One was the purchase of the water bomber. In effect, we are putting $147 million aside in order to purchase up to 36 water-bombers form Canadair in Montreal.
May I indicate that this is the first example of co-operative procurement between the federal and provincial Governments. It is fitting that this should take place because we are dealing with a typically Canadian technology. The Canadair CL-215 water bomber is known internationally as the "Canadair". It is the aircraft that is most often identified with the Canadian Aerospace Industry in the International field.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Is the Minister prepared to table some documents testifying to the comment that he just made that it is known internationally as a great airplane?

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is hardly a point of order. Hon. Members should know that there is a provision for questions following an Hon. Member's speech. Perhaps he could wait until that time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman was as well travelled as he claims, he would have known that countries including China and France refer to this aircraft as the "Canadair". It is the only aircraft manufactured specifically for waterbombing activities.
In addition to that, I announced the acceleration of the construction of the 11 Coast Guard ships. That is a program involving $780 million. We will be building six 1100 series icebreakers nav-aid tenders. We will also be building two 1050 series nav-aid tenders with icebreaking capacity and two smaller 800 series. Furthermore, we will be replacing the Labrador which is now 33 years old and is one of the fleet icebreakers of the Canadian coastguard. That involves a contract that we estimate in the vicinity of $100 million.
In sum total, the amount to be invested is approximately $780 million. Of course, that does not include the frigate program which we will be approving at the end of June or beginning of July. It does not include the DLEX, the destroyer life extension program that DND has in place for which I am letting contracts to shipyards throughout the country on a regular basis. It does not include the TRUP, the Tribal Class Update Program which has not yet been approved by Cabinet. We are dealing with sizeable amounts that will be invested by the Government of Canada in the shipbuilding industry in the very near future. In these particular instances that I have described, the criteria that has been identified for fast-tracking are being met. The major amounts of the expenditures will be expended within the next two years and the work will begin within the next six months.
In addition to that, the selection of the process of the specific projects was based upon Canadian content. We insisted that those projects which were selected had to maximize Canadian value added in order to create jobs in the Canadian marketplace. Moreover, we wanted a large number of the dollars to go into the manufacturing sector because that
is where the jobs are and where our experience has not been the best.
One would recognize that, when considering the creation of jobs, the incidence of job creation is greatest where the value added to the product of service is the greatest. In the extracting industries, the jobs tend to be fewer per dollar invested than in the manufacturing sector. We have a rule of thumb in my Department which states that if we invest $1 million in the resource extraction sector we create one job; if we invest $1 million in the manufacturing sector, we create 15 jobs. The ratio is quite impressive.
Canada's weakness in the past has been its lack of concentration on the manufacturing sector. The proof is in the pudding. When one studies our DRIE figures and breaks them down, although we have a surplus in trade, it can be seen that we have a major and growing deficit in end products. I am not talking about semi-processed goods but end products or manufactured goods. We rose to over $20 billion in end products deficit in 1981. The last figures I have show that we will not be very far from that mark for 1982. Therefore, we are looking at a deficit of $20 billion in end products in Canada.
Another rule of thumb in my Department is that for every million dollars we spend on procurement on end products we create or maintain 70 direct or indirect jobs. If you eliminated that $20 billion in end products deficit and multiplied it by the 70 jobs per million dollars expended, you would create 1.4 million jobs, which is very close to the total number of unemployed as defined by Statistics Canada today. Indeed, we must increase our activity in the manufacturing sector.
I am pleased to find that I have a very strong ally in that opinion. I read an article in Monday's Globe and Mail which was entitled "Canada at Crossroads: Crosbie. Tory Candidate Outlines His Plans". I would like to refer to some of the comments that the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) has made because I agree with them. I believe that he is at last showing his true Grit colours by espousing quite openly in his leadership campaign some of those policies that we have been developing and implementing for many years now. In dealing with manufacturing, which of course is the thrust of my speech, he said:
The Canadian Manufacturing sector faces some severe problems in the near future.
We must limit the fragmentation of the Canadian market by negotiating a Code of Conduct binding on all Governments. In particular, we must seek an agreement limiting By-Provincial procurement policies.
I agree fully with him and I have been doing that for the past two years. Indeed, I have met twice with my colleagues at the provincial level to deal with this exact issue.
The benefits we have obtained from those progressive policies have been the water bomber which I have just described. The water bomber procurement is the first prime example of strategic goods being purchased jointly by the federal and provincial Governments. We are contributing our $147 million and asking the provincial Governments to do the same. They have already indicated that they are prepared to do so.
May 3, 1983

The Hon. Member also talked about the question of world product mandating. I have been dealing with that issue since I have been Minister of Supply and Services. I have implemented world product mandating with every large corporation that has been supplying goods to the Government of Canada and doing so with a great deal of success.
We are removing any remaining tax disincentives to exports. This budget deals exactly with that. It says that for Canadians working abroad on specified activities, the current deduction for overseas employment income will be replaced by a tax credit of 80 per cent of the Canadian tax payable on up to $100,000 of such overseas income. In the past there have been some complaints that people would not want to go abroad because they face a burden on their income as a result of doing that. We had representations by exporters to put in this provision and we put it in. An amount of $180 million was put into the budget in order to promote exports.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are getting up, and that means you want me to sit down. I will be pleased to do that. But I just want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that Members of the Opposition have recognized, as I indicated initially, the excellence of this budget, and I am looking to their support when the time comes.

I would point out to the Minister that that is a contract let for the second year in a row over the objections of other businesses in the area. Is it the policy of the Government to grant contracts to reserve officers? Purportedly the Government has done so. If I can believe the Minister, he has just said that that would be

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not say in this particular sense there was a conflict of interest because I do not know this particular case. I am a bit concerned that the hon. gentleman, knowing that I was defending my Estimates in committee this morning, did not ask this question or give me notice of it so that I could provide him with a better reply. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister about the Canadair water bomber sale to which he alluded in his speech. While I share the Minister's assessment of the plane as to its quality, I cannot be quite as enthusiastic about the sale. Last week when the announcement was made, we were led to believe the sale would be for 36 water bombers. However, in the Minister's speech today he said the sale was for up to 36 water bombers. As I understand it, the federal Government's commitment is for four only at this point but for another 16 if the Provinces match the federal Government. In other words, if a province buys one, the federal Government will buy one. It seems to me that if the Provinces do not buy any of these water bombers, then it is not much of a deal at all. If some of the Provinces do not agree to buy any, then it is less of a deal than the big deal the Government would have us believe. Would the Minister care to comment on that, please?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for agreeing with me that this is the best aircraft for the purpose in the world. Often Canadians do not take sufficient pride in their own accomplishments in the technological area. I commend the hon. gentleman for recognizing that this particular aircraft is indeed very worthwhile. I invite the hon. gentleman to see a demonstration-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have seen one. The Manitoba Government flies them.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is right. The Manitoba Government has been interested in the water bombers for some time. As a matter of fact, if one looks at the experience of those Provinces that have the CL-215s, one will see how effective they have been in controlling forest fires. Manitoba and Quebec are two examples. As far as Quebec is concerned, that Government has already agreed to purchase additional numbers. The Province of Ontario is going to cabinet and will be purchasing additional numbers as well. We have every hope other Provinces will see the usefulness of the aircraft and will purchase their first aircraft. I might point out to the hon. gentleman that we were in a position where we had to put our cash on the table before

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Korchinski
the Provinces came in. We went to the Provinces with two officials. There were negotiations and the Provinces saw the necessity of acquiring a water bomber fleet. They indicated the number to us. They said to us that before they could act credibly on this matter they would have to have some indication of seriousness on the part of the Government of Canada, and until the budget was brought down there have been no indications that the money would be put on the table and that it would be made available for the procurement. Until that time it was very difficult for individual cabinets at the provincial level to start dealing with the issue. Now they are dealing with the issue and I am very optimistic they will be meeting our expectations.
The other point, of course, is that by having a production run at Canadair at Montreal one is in a position to be competitive in the international markets. Because there were so few domestic orders for the CL-215, Canadair's marketing efforts in the international marketplace were not very aggressive. Indeed, one of the conditions we have imposed in terms of this particular program is that Canadair seize this opportunity to resume aggressive international marketing in order to sell those 20 aircraft that we described in the plan we made public last Monday.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Are there other questions or comments? Debate.
The Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to make a few comments on what I call the Rip Van Winkle budget. Suddenly the Government woke up to the facts of life, suddenly it realized what was happening in the country; and suddenly in its sleep it rolled over on the other side. Suddenly the Government realized that there are out there two million people who are unemployed. To a large extent this Government contributed to that figure.
Over the years as I have watched the operation of the Liberals in office I have often seen them introduce legislation which goes to the extreme. Liberal Governments go too far and then allow considerable debate in the House, out in the country. Then they slowly withdraw. We hear Liberals, say, "Look how wonderful we are. Look at what we are doing for you." What Liberal Governments do is draw in the reins and then loosen them. It is much like going fishing. Liberals think the public will forget what they have done to them. The Liberals wonder what happened to the Gallup poll and why they are down in the polls. Can you imagine anyone who has been a lifelong Liberal losing his business, losing the result of his efforts over the years, and yet still turning to this very Government and voting Liberal again, Mr. Speaker? Why should anyone do that only to get kicked in the teeth again? After all, some of these businesses could not be sold because they are defunct, and who would buy a business going broke? Who would buy a collapsing business? Where would that businessman turn to for his retirement income? He has nowhere to turn, and suddenly the Government comes along and starts lending money. Most of us have just gone through the exercise of preparing our income tax returns. High income and low
income earners alike have to contribute toward the recovery program which the Government is initiating.
Why is it necessary to destroy the initiative and expertise of businesses, in some cases forever, and then turn around and say that it is necessary to retrain? Retrain for what? Can we imagine what students leaving high school or perhaps dropouts think about their future? They know that the Government is offering a plan but they do not know where to go. They wonder what is the future of this particular industry or that particular field. Can we imagine what they are faced with when trying to make up their minds about what to do?
All of us in our teens had to make decisions as to what we hoped to do with our lives. Oftentimes our plans did not turn out, but at least we were able to sit and ponder and hopefully plan and train ourselves for the future. It was an agonizing experience, even at the best of times, to decide in which direction to go. Can we imagine what any young student goes through today when trying to make that decision?
The Government is going to retrain and it is designating the particular fields in which to retrain. I have visited some Communist countries and I was told that once Governments decide that a person should go into a particular field he or she is stuck for life. Regardless of whether or not one likes the particular field after a few years of experience, one is stuck for life. There is no longer any room for initiative or incentive in our country because the Government has destroyed it.
Government Members talk about wrestling inflation to the ground. They did not wrestle inflation to the ground; they wrestled the people to the ground. People are flat on their backs, and the Government comes along with programs and says, "Look at these wonderful things".
A few years ago the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board came through with the LIFT Program. I referred to it as the "Lower Income For Tomorrow" program because he told farmers to take land out of production and to put it into summer fallow. Today we have another LIFT Program. This time I call it, "Lower Incentives for the Troubled". The Government still has a LIFT Program because it has a LIFT mentality.
The Government comes along and destroys incentives and then it says that it will do things for Canadians. We have a $31 billion deficit. It is spending money which it does not have. The Special Recovery Program itself will not be paid for immediately. It is to be paid for later. As if we would not notice it, it will sneak up from behind and hit us when we are not watching. It is part of the Government's "fly now pay later" program. This is exactly what the Government has been doing with its deficits. Deficits are only deferred tax.
Members of the Government seem to have a fixed mentality. They simply come up with programs, and then a few years down the road ask the people to pay for them. They think that we will not notice it, that it will just be another burden. They take great pride in their six and five program and say that it
May 3, 1983

was responsible for controlling inflation. How silly can they get? The six and five program was not responsible for controlling inflation. High interest rates made it impossible for businessmen to replace the stock on their shelves. High interest rates stopped farmers from purchasing machinery. High interest rates caused manufacturers to wonder whether or not they should expand, and of course they did not. When they use that type of mechanism they do not take into account the fact that people make plans. When they make plans, they anticipate that their incomes will be such and such. They look at their returns for the past few years, they know what they are manufacturing or producing, they anticipate the market and perhaps calculate the price. They know what their revenues should be and what some of their fixed costs will be. They plan over a period of years. Then they buy pieces of equipment based upon the fact that the interest rate will be 12 per cent. They project five years down the road and, lo and behold, the Government intercedes and slaps on a 23 per cent interest rate. How can such individuals, as intelligent as they may be with all their expertise and knowledge in their fields, cope with that situation? What for?
Today we have to reverse our thinking. We will not find such people. Does the Government think they are silly enough to go back into the fields, uncertain as they are as to what it will do next? If the Government had wanted to provide these people with initiatives, it should have taken into account some of the purchases which were calculated on the basis of their projections and anticipated expenditures. It could have categorized the interest rate and taken those purchases into account. It was possible. Those who had already made purchases based upon anticipated income could have been left at a fixed rate of interest. Another level could have been set for those people who had to replace inventory or stock. If it wanted to create incentive, it could have increased the rate at another level and made it possible for businessmen to stay in business. It could have taken into account the undesirability of an over-expanded or over-heated economy. It could have said that it would restrict the money available and told people not to expand at this particular time because inflation was a great problem. It could have restricted it without having to destroy business at the same time. That would have retained many people in jobs and many businesses in place. Instead, the Government pounced on everyone-the ones with low incomes, the ones with high incomes, the ones who had purchased refrigerators or some other essential for their homes. It pummelled manufacturers that had been in business for many years, and then it provided a little incentive. It gave a few grants here and there. It said, "We will be good to you and give you grants in order to create jobs". It was a kind of hat trick.
I recall a man by the name of John Turner standing across the way as the Minister of Finance. At that time he introduced a measure to remove the ceiling on farm improvement loans. The press says that some day John Turner will be the Leader of the Liberal Party. The Liberals may want him, but I certainly do not want him around this place. When he removed the ceiling, he said that a lot of money would be available. We
The Budget-Mr. Korchinski
warned him of the danger of removing that 5 per cent ceiling, but he said there would be more money available.
For a while his prediction came true. Then the rate rose from 5 per cent to 7 per cent and then 8 per cent. People grumbled a bit, but they were still accommodating. When it shot up to 12 per cent, people became jittery, wondering where the economy was going, but they adjusted. When it reached 23 per cent, lo and behold, they could not pay the interest, never mind the principal. The banks, Financial institutions and the Farm Credit Corporation said there was a lot of money and that to get it, you need only sign on the dotted line. Today these same institutions are calling in the loans saying, "That's it. There is no more money".
What happened to the money that John Turner predicted would be available? If you look at Hansard for that time, you will see that that is what was said. What has happened to that money?
I receive many calls and letters from people in financial trouble. Farmers are going bankrupt. They are being taken to court and their assets are being sold. A Bill has been introduced by a Private Member to try to help those who took the advice of the Government and the banks.
I have had experience with the banks. When I was refused money by one banker, I went to another banker. I am sick and tired of these bankers who obviously are not accommodating. They will not even listen to you. They ask why you were not a customer previously. That banker may not realize that I am sick and tired of trying to deal with my former banker who is no longer accommodating but only interested in a profit for his branch. His interest is not my interest, but I have to live with it. When you try another bank, you get the same result. It is as though there were a network between the banks.
My constituents who call and write to me are telling me the same story. Over the years one of my constituents, a farmer, purchased land from other farmers. He has created jobs in that area. He has built up assets. Because of inflation, the land value went up to $2.5 million. He controlled a large part of that area. All of a sudden he had to dispose of everything. In the process, he will put a dozen companies out of business because he was their major customer.
The Government does not have to use the taxpayers' money. It need only talk to the banks. I have written to the Minister with regard to the Small Business Development Bond. His reply was that he cannot interfere. If he cannot talk to the bankers, who can? Certainly not the man who needs the money. It is only as a last resort that people write to their Member of Parliament, who in turn contacts the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde), the same Minister who says he cannot do anything about it. The Minister can do something about it. He can ask the banks to be more accommodating, to allow a little more time. It is not necessary to tax those earning the minimum wage in order to make a recovery. This can be done without using the taxpayers' money if only the Government

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Korchinski
will take the initiative. The Government is slapping the wrist of the businessman. It is not able to talk to the bankers.
I now want to deal with the housing aspect. The Government announced an increase of 2,500 units in the social housing area. This is a sensitive area. As soon as you talk about social housing, people immediately think of the penniless and the destitute. I have access to information which leads me to believe that when there is a vacancy, it is filled by the next in line, even though that person may be borderline and might better fit into another scheme.
Once someone is in such a housing unit, you cannot put him out. Then there are those who, knowing something about an individual in social housing, because they do not have as much revenue, believe that they should be entitled to social housing as well. Because one person is entitled to social housing, there could soon be a line-up of people who believe they are entitled to it as well because they think it is Government policy. Therefore, the Government must be very careful. It may be necessary to have a rental supplement or possibly some kind of means test and not have to use the taxpayers' money as a subsidy. I understand the average subsidy is approximately $4,000 per unit. I understand that not in all cases is the taxpayers' money used for people who are in desperate need of shelter and have no other way of obtaining it.

speechtext: Order. I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member, but the time provided for his speech has expired.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member. With regard to the need for housing, has the Hon. Member any comments on how the budget could provide incentives to home buyers without adding to the budgetary deficit?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are several ways of accomplishing this. One item sadly missing from the budget was an insurance scheme so that those having to renew their mortgages will not be saddled with the high interest rate simply because they must renew their mortgage at a time when interest rates are high. I asked the Miniter in the House whether any consideration was being given to this. I believe that an averaging out scheme can be accomplished without using any taxpayers' money. This does not necessarily have to be compulsory nor does it have to cost the Government-when I say Government, I mean the taxpayers-money because additional insurance can be taken out at a small additional premium to ensure that over the next few years your mortgage will not suddenly be increased from 12 per cent to 19 per cent or 20 per cent.
If the Government could work out the details of such a scheme, then the people who pay for the mortgages and pay for the premiums would not be playing what I call "renewable roulette". Renewable roulette means that if your mortgage rates are high, you are stuck paying that high rate. In my own case, I had a mortgage at 12% per cent, and lo and behold, the
time for renewal came and I had to renew at 16% per cent. If my mortgage were to come due today, I would be lucky. But it is not so. In other words, it is possible to work out such a scheme.
While I am on my feet, I would just like to comment on one other aspect and that is the $10,000-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can comment on that because the Minister of Finance mentioned that in his budget and suggested that this would be one of those megaprojects that he talks about. On the one hand he will create jobs by building a railway, he calls it double-tracking or fast-tracking, but where will he get the money to do this? He will get the money from the farmer.
You know that the farmer is one of those enterprising individuals who does not need to be spurred on. He does not need to have salesmen knocking at his door. He is looking for salesmen because he always has need for a battery, for a tire, for electrical equipment, for new machinery, for new saws, for new hammers, for new refrigeration equipment, you name it. The farmer has need of everything. His needs do not fall into one particular category. A homeowner can only buy so many items, but out on the farm it is an entirely different story. Every industry benefits from the farmer.
Lo and behold, the Government wants to withdraw out of Saskatchewan alone $1 million a year that it claims will help create jobs. Why withdraw that money? That money might best be left in the hands of the farmer because he is a great purchaser. Why do you think farmers are so deeply in debt to the Farm Credit Corporation and to the banks? Because they enjoy buying products that will enable them to work as efficiently as anybody else does. In fact, the farmer is more efficient because he has been buying implements.
The Government's program will supposedly create jobs, but it will create jobs for only a few years. In the meantime, the program will destroy the established farmer. I personally know farmers who are hanging on by their fingertips. The Government is going to take more money away from that individual who is a great spender in order to create jobs. That again is a typical Liberal philosophy: take away and then give back.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchinski).
I certainly do not think that pessimistic speeches like the one we just heard are going to help Canada's economy. Anyone
May 3, 1983

who reads the newspapers will see that this budget, which has been called by some people the key to Canada's future, can give the economy a boost if we are all willing to give it a chance.
When the Hon. Member said the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) should have taken action and spoken to the banks' representatives, I would have liked him to give us further details, because he did not indicate what the Minister of Finance was supposed to say to the banks. Was he referring to the need for lower interest rates in Canada compared with the United States? I may remind him that, when he says the Minister of Finance is mortgaging Canadians, in Canada savings represent about 13 per cent of disposable income, which is twice as much as in the United States. The message given by the Minister of Finance is a message of optimism which appeals to the private sector and is aimed at developing our economy.
I would have liked to hear what the Hon. Member has to say about interest rates.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought I had made that clear, though the Hon. Member thinks I did not. Perhaps my message did not come across as clearly as I had hoped. At that time I did say that I expected the Minister of Finance to sit down with the bankers and tell them that rather than foreclose and take these people to court, they should just give them an extension and let the farmers work out their own salvation, give them a little more time. There is no point in destroying an enterprise that has been built up through hard work, borrowed money and a lot of sweat, only to find out that another job must be created. Rather than calling in the debts immediately, all the banks need to do is to give the borrower more time. I suppose the banks are entitled to operate their own business, but it is strange that the banks spend so much money in other countries. They lost a lot of money in other countries and now they are trying to recover it on the backs of the enterprising individuals who create the jobs in Canada. If the banks can lose money outside of Canada, then they can take a chance on Canadians. That is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said. All I am asking the banks to do is to take a chance on Canadians.
