subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that for well over a week now, Hon. Members, especially on the Government side, have been very pleased not only with the kind of budget that was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) but also with the enthusiasm it has generated across the country. I think that a sensible person reading the general comments made in various circles would agree that this budget is indeed a budget of hope and economic recovery, and also one that gives Canadians an opportunity to put the economy on the right track by using the comprehensive measures it contains. I think Canadians were ready for this budget.
Mr. Speaker, for the information of my colleagues, I would like to quote part of a speech made by Mr. Frazee at the Canadian Club of Montreal on April 25, that is, after the budget was brought down. Mr. Frazee, who never minces his words when referring to the economic policies of the Liberal Party of Canada, said that on the whole, the budget deserved praise. It acknowledged that creating permanent jobs was exclusively up to the private sector, and it would undoubtedly create a favourable climate in that sector. Since Mr. Frazee is one of many businessmen who for several years has been urging Ottawa to take action in this respect, I must say that I am very pleased. The construction industry needed strong stimulation, and it received it. Protectionism had to be firmly rejected and it was. The specific problems of farmers were taken into consideration. A short respite was granted to the energy sector. The mining industry and research and development were stimulated and the purchase of capital goods encouraged.
Mr. Speaker, in other words, the wishes of all Canadians who were consulted in recent months by the Minister of Finance, who managed to hold one of the broadest and most comprehensive rounds of consultations among all social groups in Canada and who produced this budget-the wishes of all these people were given consideration, and I think the budget is able to create a climate that will restore confidence to all our constituents.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal more specifically with two measures that interested me in this budget, since my colleagues have already had a chance to discuss other aspects. First, however, I would like to point that this economic recovery budget will provide for direct job creation in the short term

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mrs. Hervieux-Payette
and stimulate investment as well, with $2.4 billion being earmarked for longer term investments, and all this without cutting social programs. Mr. Speaker, I was one of those who worried that family allowances might be affected by the budget. A number of groups had emphasized the need for a more restrictive reallocation of funds, but I think that the principle of universality was nevertheless maintained by the Minister of Finance, and as a Liberal, I am very proud of this fact.
The same applies to pensions, Mr. Speaker. The Government did not yield to the temptation to select groups that were in serious trouble, and we have been given the assurance that the income supplement for pensioners will remain fully indexed. I believe that this recovery budget has remained true to the traditional concept of liberalism, which is that the poor should not have to suffer because of the country's economic problems and that economic recovery is to be achieved by harnessing the efforts of all members of society.
Personally, I find that one of the dynamic aspects of this budget is the measures that will stimulate recovery in the construction industry. The latest figures published April 26, 1983, show that Canadians are gaining confidence and that a drop in interest rates, as a result of our successful monetary policy, means that the forecast for 1984 is for from 165,000 to
185,000	units compared with 80,000 in 1982. 1 think that is very significant and that this will not only help to stimulate the construction industry, which is the driving force of the economy, but also all related sectors such as electrical appliances and home furnishings. In this area, the Minister of Finance kept his word and introduced measures that will remain in effect from April 19 until December 31, 1984, including the possibility for Canadians to save up to $10,000 of their income tax free for the purpose of building a home. As a precautionary measure, the Minister has maintained the $3,000 program for the time being, but since the transition period will be very short, I think the emphasis should be on the $10,000 plan. This proposal is not discriminatory. It is aimed at all those who want to build a home, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, that, as forecast by the Royal Bank, Canadian men and women will be confident enough to build these 180,000 homes in the coming year, thus providing regular, satisfying and well paid jobs to Canadians throughout the country.
Those who were well advised to invest in a Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan before April 19, 1983 will, of course, benefit from a proposal which will encourage the purchase of consumer goods, and I believe that this program will be very challenging. Those who had already thought of buying a home but had not yet done so and who would now like to use what they had invested in an RHOSP to purchase furniture, appliances and other furnishing for their home, will now be able to use the money they have saved over the years tax free; in this regard, I share the hope of the Minister of Finance that those Canadians will buy Canadian in the knowledge that our
Canadian industry always strives for competitive quality and prices.
Mr. Speaker, the second matter I want to deal with is another very dynamic program which will be implemented later this year and which, in my opinion, will enable Canadian businessmen to put their business back on a sound financial footing. I am talking, of course, about the Special Recovery Share Purchase Tax Credit. After presiding on a House subcommittee on finance which produced a unanimous report on this subject, in June 1982, I believe that in the end we can be proud of the fact that the Minister of Finance decided to introduce this incentive which will encourage Canadians to purchase equity in Canadian businesses. We have known trying times when interest rates were going up and the only alternative was to wait for the demand to go down. If we ever have to go through that experience again, and I trust this will never happen, I believe that a better business capital structure will allow us to absorb such pressures much more easily and at much less cost and that measures such as this one will enable us to meet more than one objective.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, if Canadians begin to invest through equity in their own companies, not only will they benefit from the increased value of their equity through dividends-taxable, of course, but not at prohibitive rates-they will also be able to promote their ideas and combine their efforts, particularly if they are employees. That was the idea behind our Committee on employee participation in profits, equity and decisionmaking. When we tabled our report, Mr. Speaker, we were convinced that the Government would have to introduce tax measures to spur business financing simply through investment of profits in companies and the issue of shares to employees instead of higher wages, something which makes competition ever more difficult.
Mr. Speaker, the measure which was adopted by the Minister of Finance will lower the cost of new shares issued to investors and make it a more interesting proposition. Investors will be allowed to use that 25 per cent tax credit to reduce their federal income tax. I suggest that the figure of 25 per cent is very significant, showing as it does that the Minister of Finance is firmly committed to the economic recovery which is the central thrust of this budget. I think that the budget amply demonstrates the will of the Liberal Government to guarantee the recovery through the private sector.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would remind businessmen and small companies in my riding-or even larger corporations which are sometimes already financed through shares issued on the public market-that even private companies are eligible under the program, which will make it easier for employees to sit at the bargaining table with management officials and have a say in the decision making process. In my opinion, we cannot emphasize strongly enough the fact that an incentive mechanism such as the special tax credit will pave the way for much closer co-operation between labour and management.
May 3, 1983

Mr. Speaker, the budget contains many other outstanding measures. I wanted to single out the construction recovery program and the special recovery capital projects because I was among those who were concerned with the lack of job creation measures for groups of workers who found themselves in difficulty. I think that the budget meets all my aspirations as a Member and, thanks to this initiative, I hope that all businessmen-all men and women in Quebec as far as I am concerned-will do their share and avail themselves of the measures in the Lalonde budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Questions, comments? Debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to commend my colleagues who have participated in this debate and who have made very valuable contributions.
My remarks relate to development measures contained in the budget and focus on the Department of Regional Economic Expansion which we refer to as DREE. The division of DREE into two parts and its burial in two other Departments of Government, is not a matter of rejoicing in the areas of Canada which suffer most from problems of regional disparity. The Government is announcing the funeral of DREE, not the celebration of the birth of a more effective instrument of regional development. Those of us who mourn DREE's demise do so for the lack of direct successor. We are not blind to imperfections in DREE's concept and execution. Nor, on the other hand, do we seize this occasion merely to blame the Government for all the deficiencies of DREE. It is imperative, however, to ask what we can learn from the experiences of DREE and from the Government's regional development policies generally over the last ten to 15 years. Only in light of answers to these questions can we judge the appropriateness of measures introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and by the Minister responsible for DREE in his excellent comments a little earlier in this debate.
In 1969, the Government made a strong commitment to reduce regional economic disparities with the formation of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. The Department's expenditures expressed as a percentage of gross general expenditure peaked in 1970-71 at $330.8 million, or 2.1 per cent of gross general expenditure. These expenditures have declined each year since then, hovering at about 1.1 per cent of gross general expenditure in each year since 1978-79. In terms of constant 1971 dollars, departmental expenditures in the Atlantic region peaked in 1970-71 at $184 million. They declined to $108 million in 1977-78. During that period, DREE's spending in Atlantic Canada declined by 41.2 percent. Despite all the rhetoric concerning current and future initiatives, the record clearly shows that the Government's commitment to regional economic expansion has been severely diminished in recent years.
The Budget-Mr. Howie
Let us look at some of the lessons of DREE. There is no lack of documentation on the subject: annual departmental reports, specially commissioned evaluations, and coincidentally-since it was not done in anticipation of DREE's demise-the report of the Senate Finance Committee on Government Policy and Regional Development. Differences of opinion exist within these documents, but there is also a remarkable degree of consensus. Clearly, the effectiveness of incentives to regional economic development is tied closely to other Departmental policies and activities. There have been many cases where two policies or programs have worked directly against each other. But beyond that, there has been a generally unfavourable climate for regional development, created by measures not specifically formulated with an eye to reducing regional disparities. Transportation policy is a good example. Just when a revolution in communications technology would make it possible for firms to locate head offices away from the largest population centres, the Government guts the regional passenger transportation system in the Maritimes.
The tax structure in this country, to the extent that it has discouraged risk and innovation, has actually worked against new initiatives in less developed regions. Government procurement policies have systematically discriminated against smaller firms. The targets of regional development policies have not always been thoroughly defined. There has clearly been a political temptation to draw the circle too widely. The inclusion of a huge population centre negates the object of incentives for firms to locate some distance from large makets.
In economic development there are federal responsibilities, provincial responsibilities, and shared responsibilities. The provincial Governments in the wealthier Provinces are better able to discharge their responsibilities than are Governments of less wealthy Provinces. The General Development Agreements recognized this and provided for assistance from the federal Government to less wealthy Provinces to help them in their development efforts. The weakness of the GDA was that it did not provide for the integration of programs in the area of federal jurisdiction into the total development effort of the Province. Divided responsibility for economic development should be recognized, and the need for co-ordinated federal and provincial efforts should also be recognized, so that all development activity is oriented to the achievement of common objectives.
The federal Government should have a primary interest in regional economic development since only through an effective federal regional development effort can Canadians in all parts of the country achieve reasonably similar employment and income levels. Furthermore, in the less wealthy Provinces, it is only with federal Government assistance that smaller areas of high unemployment and low income can move toward national standards.
With respect to research and development, it is essential to close the technology gap between richer and poorer regions. Once our most skilled people are able to stay in the poorer regions, we will begin to achieve the critical mass needed for further innovation and expansion. Scientific and technical

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Howie
research and development simply must take place within the regions if they are to address the particular needs and opportunities which exist there for economic expansion. The Government, with the co-operation of provincial Governments, can foster this kind of regional opportunity. It is in this light, that the Government's stalling on a project such as the Maritime forestry complex in Fredericton is inexcusable, all the more so when the declared reasons for this stalling are so blatantly partisan and when the Government is ready to go ahead with a similar project in Thailand.
DREE followed a sound strategy when it focused on growth centres within depressed regions, but in latter years has signalled a departure from the practice of building on strengths. We have a classic example in New Brunswick where the Fredericton, Saint John, Moncton triangle was excluded from the 50 per cent investment tax incentive credit. The Government's scatter-gun kind of approach has often been inefficient and unreliable. It has occasionally involved heavy expenditure on infrastructure and incentives, only to have the project collapse or require permanent subsidization because of particular localized conditions in an industry or a company. The case by case approach has also inevitably ignored or conflicted with provincial planning and priorities. It is not surprising in this regard, that DREE's greatest successes have occurred under the auspices of the General Development Agreements.
We have learned from DREE that the best investments of Government funds are generally in viable, productive enterprises. DREE grants have found consistently better returns when used for expansion and modernization as opposed to start-ups. We need more effort to determine which are viable manufacturing enterprises in the long run-usually those related to the resource base of the region-and more willingness to promote the appropriate market research and management and manpower training. Apart from infrastructure, planning has been too much of the short-term variety. Again, we have been up against political temptations, as even a Senate Committee with a Liberal majority has admitted. Ultimately, only a viable manufacturing enterprise has the potential to move a depressed region toward self-sufficiency.
Transfers of various kinds are unquestionably necessary to ensure to all Canadians a satisfactory standard of living and acceptable social and educational services. But study after study demonstrates that transfer payments alone just find their way back to the wealthier parts of the country. They do not have a permanently stimulative effect, and they do nothing about the causes of regional disparity. Even the well-intended policy of moving some federal bureaucratic establishments out of Ottawa to the regions had a very limited effect on local demand, especially beyond the construction phase. We have learned from DREE that the goal of regional development must be to lessen dependency. This is the only permanent way to narrow down disparities. This approach is unfortunately being impaired by the federal Government's continuing deficit crisis.
In the fat years, the Government's generous transfer programs promoted dependency. Now that Ottawa is having to cut back, it is picking fights with the Provinces over medicare and post-secondary education-in short, finding any possible pretext for financial retrenchment. Tragically, despite many genuine accomplishments, DREE has scarcely made a dent in the problem of dependency. With these lessons of DREE in mind, Mr. Speaker, I would like to outline some of my specific concerns regarding the breakup of DREE and the new initiatives for regional development which have been introduced in the federal budget and elaborated by the Minister responsible for DREE.
First, to replace DREE in part with the Ministry of State responsible for economic regional development and to require it to inflict a developmental dimension on other Departments of Government is like asking a fly to chase an elephant. The fanfare that has preceded MSERD is, I fear, little more than bureaucratic jargon. Unless the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) personally heads MSERD and unless he personally leads the attack on regional disparity, line Departments in times of restraint will not accept any challenge other than the existing bare bones of their responsibilities. The absence of a single Department or Minister exclusively committed to regional development does not augur well. The mandate to foster development in all regions is double-talk. It is the negation of a concerted attack on regional disparity. In that sense it can truly be said that MSERD may be absurd.
The principle that all Government Departments should be sensitive to regional needs is fine in theory, and particularly appropriate now that regional equality is a goal enshrined in the Constitution. But it is meaningless without a specific designation of responsibility within each Department. We have no assurance that such a designation will be made. I am specifically concerned about how, after all the bureaucratic shuffling has been accomplished and areas of responsibility redesignated, certain obvious priorities for regional development are going to be realized. One of these priorities is the identification of possible foreign markets and the establishment of contact with potential foreign joint investors who already have their own market contacts. Yet that portion of the old Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce with its international expertise is now going to External Affairs, which is not likely to give much attention to the needs of, for example, the Atlantic region, unless it is specifically directed to do so.
Another major area of concern is the General Development Agreements. The decision of the Government to allow existing GDAs and the subsidiary agreements under the umbrella provisions of the GDAs to expire on termination is indeed regrettable. Nothing could be simpler than the General Development Agreements themselves, and nothing could be more appropriate to the needs of the areas being served by the subsidiary agreements than those agreements which, in fact, are the product of negotiation and study by the two levels of Government involved.
May 3, 1983

Now it is clear that the Government has less determination than ever to co-ordinate its initiatives with those of the Provinces. It has no designated successor to the GDAs. It proposes a Regional Development Fund, which invites a political and bureaucratic free-for-all, the search for winners rather than a consistent long-term policy.
When we discuss disparities, the Atlantic region comes first to mind because its underdevelopment is long-standing and pervasive in contrast to pockets of underdevelopment within wealthier regions forced into temporary economic hardship caused by specific dislocations such as market demand or changes in technology. It is therefore appropriate for us to focus our efforts in this region. There are other reasons as well. Historically, the Atlantic region has been a victim not only of natural economic forces but also of political decisions, going back at least to the First World War. These political factors have been well-documented by historians and Royal Commissions, and I need not dwell on old grievances.
Politically and culturally, the Atlantic Provinces are identifiable societies with historic roots, a record of substantial contributions to the life of all Canada and the collective will and capacity to reverse the trend toward stifling dependency which has characterized their recent past. In our generation, we have witnessed the remarkable revitalization accomplished by our neighbouring society in Quebec. The support of the federal Government has been crucial to that revival.
I would strongly insist that while smaller, less powerful politically and less developed industrially than Quebec was, even at the start of the quiet revolution, the Maritime communities are equally worthy of such consideration. To deny that consideration would constitute clear evidence of discrimination, to use the term which certain Hon. Members opposite are fond of using when their ambitions are frustrated. I would like to believe that the bold new programs and initiatives announced by the Government will conscientiously avoid that kind of discrimination. But I do not see assurances that they will.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the Hon. Member who just concluded his comments. I would like his view on one of the observations he made. If I understand him correctly, he has the view that there are limited permanent benefits from relocation of federal Government Departments or sections of federal Government Departments. I suppose I have a vested interest in this matter, but in my view the effect is exactly the opposite in that at the beginning you have the additional salary dollars going into a particular area. That naturally creates demand for goods and services both for the Department and also for the additional employees working in the area. I wonder if the Hon. Member might clarify exactly what he means by little or limited permanent benefits?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Minister for his question. He correctly interpreted it as being limited because there is certainly a benefit from any Government Department relocation in terms of salaries, personnel and employment, and most particularly in terms of initial construction. I use the
The Budget-Mr. Howie
adjective "limited" quite advisedly because I have differentiated in my remarks between a Government Department and industry. An industry generates other line industries, perhaps small component parts industries in terms of spin-offs, and other industries. There are differing estimates as to the job creation factor; for every one in industry, it is five outside in terms of spin-offs. For Government Departments, it is one in and two out. Government Departments buy supplies for individuals, some centrally and some locally, but they do not have quite the magnitude of impact that an industrial development would have in terms of buying primary products, components or elements which can be reshaped, remanufactured with value added, and create more jobs through this stimulation. Certainly we in the Maritime Provinces very much welcome both factors, but the point of my address was this. The Maritime Provinces have approximately 47 per cent of their gross revenues coming in the form of transfer payments from Ottawa. We desperately need a tax base established by secondary manufacturing in order to enable our Governments through increased tax revenue, both personal and corporate, to increase their incomes and decrease their dependency on the central Government. We cannot tax Government Departments, and this is one salient difference and another reason why I used the word "limited".
I appreciate the impact that Departments have in that region, particularly of Veterans Affairs in Charlottetown. It employs many people and does have a good impact. As well, there is the Pensions Branch in New Brunswick. These are important, necessary and very welcome employers in the Maritimes.
But we also need industries. We need an industrial base which we do not have now. As the Hon. Member knows, the Island is heavily dependent economically on its primary resource base. A primary resource based economy is the first hit, the hardest hit and the last to recover in times of a recession. We most certainly need all the help we can get, and I thank the Hon. Member for his contribution.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have a brief supplementary question. Would the Hon. Member not agree that the relocation of Departments and agencies to the area would not only provide salary dollars and expenditures in the area but create the potential for the establishment of a processing or manufacturing industry? Would he agree that a relocated Department or agency could foster the development of a small industry in an area where the demand might not have existed at the time? In other words, I do not disagree with his observations in terms of getting the maximum spin-off, but would he not agree that the relocation can in fact complement the development of that demand which could lead to further manufacturing opportunities within Atlantic Canada, for example?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I certainly agree with the Hon. Member that an increase in the consumer population can stimulate and create a market for industrial development.

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Ogle
We have two basic concepts. One is that if we are to look at efficiency in terms of industry, we must have regard for industries that can be built in terms of their optimum capacity. Many of our resource based industries, particularly in forestry, not only require our domestic markets but world markets as well in order to operate to optimum capacity. Industries that are looking at world capacity require very different incentives than industries that require domestic market capacity.
We certainly have need for both in the Atlantic Provinces. We still are net importers of much of our major food components. There is substantial room for expansion in this particular field.
Our fisheries industry has not been mentioned in the budget but it has been shown that our processing plants have a lot of unused capacity. Yet our fisheries industry is a substantial importer of deck hardware, navigational aids and equipment. This is where the big money is and it is another area in which I think we can move toward a transformation of the unused capacity that exists in this particular primary product area to a manufacturing concept that can employ more Canadians who live in the Atlantic Provinces.
I certainly agree with the Hon. Minister that we have a great need to increase our consumer demand and population in this regard. That essentially was his question and I do agree with him. I expect, seeing him nod, that he agrees with me that we also need a secondary manufacturing base.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak during the last hour of the budget debate which has been taking place for six days. We will soon be voting on the budget.
I would like to direct my remarks to two areas that have been touched upon by other Members but not explained, in my opinion, in any great detail. Members from both sides of the House have particular areas of concern that affect them and their constituencies. As well, Members on the Government side have special areas of concern either in the role of Minister or Parliamentary Secretary to a Minister.
Hon. Members and Canadians will remember that at the beginning of this year the social action department of the Canadian Catholic Conference of Bishops presented a statement which concerned ethical reflections on the present economic situation. As we are all aware, that document received a great deal of discussion. Many supported all of its contents and some supported certain sections while others disagreed with certain sections, with the entire document or with the whole basic principle that the Bishops had no right to speak on economic matters. While I have a special link with the Bishops, it is my personal belief that they do have a right to speak on moral matters, economic matters and social matters which concern the lives of people.
Yesterday, the American Catholic Bishops spoke very strongly against the arms build-up. There will be Americans who will be upset about that today. I believe that the Bishops had a perfect right and a duty to speak on a subject that is
causing so much immorality, that is, the destruction of the planet.
The Bishops' statement in Canada had two basic principles upon which they built their reflections. The first concerned the preferential option for the poor, afflicted and oppressed. The Bishops said:
In the tradition of the prophets, Jesus dedicated his ministry to bringing "good news to the poor" and "liberty to the oppressed". As Christians, we are called to follow Jesus by identifying with the victims of injustice, by analysing the dominant attitudes and structures that cause human suffering, and by actively supporting the poor and oppressed in their struggles to transform society. For, as Jesus declared, "when you did it unto these, the least of my brethren, you did it unto me".
The second principle that the Bishops' statement was structured upon was this:
The second principle concerns the special value and dignity of human work in God's plan for Creation. It is through the activity of work that people are able to exercise their creative spirit, realize their human dignity, and share in Creation. By interacting with fellow workers in a common task, men and women have an opportunity to further develop their personalities and sense of self-worth. In so doing, people participate in the development of their society and give meaning to their existence as human beings. Indeed, the importance of human labour is illustrated in the life of Jesus who was himself a worker, "a craftsman like Joseph of Nazareth".
In light of those two principles, I would like to speak on what this budget has done in general and whether it fulfilled what the Bishops were speaking about when they issued their statement.
The first principle of preferential option for the poor is one that has developed in Latin America in the last 20 years. It is a social principle based primarily on the teachings of the Catholic Church and others as well, but particularly on the social teachings of the Pope. That principle was that when it came to the necessity of taking an option in any particular economic situation, the option would be for the poor, unemployed, aged, sick, children, and those without power. They should be looked after first, and the other areas of society could then have the opportunity to be cared for.
I suggest that in the preparation of the budget that principle was never even considered. The unemployed, the aged, the students without jobs and those without power in the society are still without power and not looked after.
The Minister has indicated that the unemployment rate is not going to change. The budget is not directed toward changing the number of people who would go to work. The budget is directed at starting a stimulus in the economy somehow but the number of people still suffering as underprivileged will remain the same. Perhaps for all intents and purposes the number could go up. Twelve per cent of the work force is out of work. The Government admits that unemployment is not going to go below 11 per cent for four years. Again, that is only a supposition. The figure could still rise.
In Canada at the present time, as you are aware, Mr. Speaker, and as Members of the House are aware, the top 20 per cent of Canadians receive 42.5 per cent of the total personal income, while the bottom 20 per cent receive only 4 per cent.
May 3, 1983

It is figures such as these that indicate to me at least that this budget does not change the basic situation in Canada and that the poor are still the ones who will suffer because of what the budget does not do.
On the other hand, to show that the preferential option has not been made on behalf of the poor, the Government is giving $2.67 billion in corporate tax breaks while personal income tax, again taking in a mass of people at the bottom, the poor in society, will be up by $3.5 billion and sales taxes will be up by $2.4 billion over the next four years. This indicates that the people at the bottom, the poor, are the ones who will benefit least from the budget.
The second principle which the Bishops outlined in their document of January is the principle that human work is a right for people. A person cannot really grow, perform his or her role and be perfect unless he or she has the opportunity to do something creative and to do it in companionship with other people.
The burden of just being unemployed, the anger of a person who cannot do anything is a terrible thing. I am sure anybody who does his constituency work knows what it is like to have people who are unemployed come to see him. These are people who have looked for work, have been to the employment agency and have tried to get a job but cannot, and this is dreadful. They carry a tremendous burden. They feel they are worthless. They say they are no good. I hear it said all the time. I am sure you have heard it said, Mr. Speaker, because I am sure you are doing your constituency work. It is that feeling that shows the second principle has not been respected and that in this budget the right for all people to have a job has not been respected.
The budget indicates that businesses would benefit. I have heard many Members say in the House, and Members who represent the business sector have all quite clearly said, that businesses will benefit. The bishops have warned that even if companies recover and increase their profit margins, the additional revenues are likely to be reinvested in more labour saving technology, exported to other countries or spent on market speculation or luxury goods. If money moves in that direction, it does not necessarily mean that more people will work. All of us who have any sense at all of how technology is moving into society are aware that jobs will be harder and harder to find and create in the present economic situation unless it is planned that everyone in society will have a job. It may mean in the future that we will have to start looking for areas of activity in human life that we do not classify as jobs now. We will have to find other ways in which all of the wealth that a country like Canada can produce can be redistributed in a way that all people will benefit from it in a just way. At the same time they must experience the value, the feeling and the knowledge that they are doing something creative. The distribution should not be simply because a person does not have a traditional kind of job. There will be less and less of the traditional kinds of jobs. Another way will have to be found so that distribution will take place. In that respect I would say the
The Budget-Mr. Ogle
budget does not fulfil the principles outlined by the Bishops in their statement of early January, 1983.
I want to speak now for a few minutes about my area as a critic, which is international aid and development, and how the budget has affected that area as far as I can see it. First, I was happy to see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) did pay some attention to the international scene in his budget. Unfortunately it was more of a passing scene. Likewise I would be critical of the Bishops' statement on the ground that, although, to my mind, it correctly identified the fact that the problem Canada was suffering from was not unique, that it was an international problem, in their judgment of how the problems could be remedied they did not in my view address it in an international way. I criticize the Biships' statement for being incomplete in that respect.
The Minister in his budget speech did outline some points on the international scene. Fie indicated the interdependence of nations and that we cannot forget the least fortunate ones. I might mention, for instance, the North-South dialogue in which the problem of the recession, the depression, or whatever you want to call it, that has taken place was correctly phro-phesied and seen prior to its occurrence by the independent committee under Willy Brandt. This North-South study was done several years ago. That same group of people are now working on their own because their commission has officially come to an end. They produced just recently a new little booklet called "Common Crisis" which updated their previous positions on how the world has to tie together-the North and the South, the rich and the poor-to bring about some kind of human existence to the whole planet. In this booklet, to which the Minister alluded in his budget, they indicate the area of trade. There were other areas not specifically mentioned by the Minister in relation to the international situation because the Brandt people indicated it is necessary to have employment resolved in an international manner. Aid would have to be looked at in an international way, and the great problem of international credit and the massive debt load of the Third World creates a special problem. The debt load of the South amounts to at least $600 billion or more. Many of the countries that were just beginning to develop and were making a few breakthroughs have fallen behind and have almost crashed under the load of their debt. This is not only true of little countries, which are in the worst situation, but it is true also of large countries such as Brazil, Mexico, Nigeria and others. Even though they have wealth and an economic base that was beginning to build, that same economic base has fallen, it fell in the last year. All those different setbacks because of the North-South link will affect Canada as well. These things are not mentioned in the budget as far as I can see.
The Minister stated in the little budget booklet entitled "Budget in brief' that tariff rates will be looked at in a special way. On page 14 we find:
Lower rates of customs duty on some $10 million in annual imports from developing countries, under the General Preferential Tariff, are being implemented as recommended by the Tariff Board.

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Ogle
That is good. However, let us put that in relation to the fact that the capacity of developing countries to import has fallen $100 billion, according to the Brandt people. That is what the developing countries are not able to buy from or trade with those who are rich, in other words, the North.
Now we come to how Canadians in general look upon what Canada should be doing as a country in its aid to the developing world. This is a complicated and large field. The difficulty we have right now is in knowing where the Canadian aid program is going. We have not had a president of CIDA for almost six months. 1 feel the frustration of the people in CIDA because they do not have a president to enunciate clear policies.
In the past year, in non-governmental organizations, such as church organizations, the YMCA and various funds for the care of children in the developing world, Canadians gave more percentage-wise than the year before, even though it was during a period of recession. Canadian people still have a generous attitude toward help. That is an extremely important matter of which the Government should be aware. We have heard Members of the House speak against aid. They have the right to speak against some aid because it is not aiding anyone other than some company in Canada. Canadians are interested in aid and have shown their interest by raising private donations to help other countries in the developing world. I have been told by people in charge of non-governmental organizations that that is generally the case across the board.
It is important for the Government to remember, when it talks about international institutions and replenishing the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank or any one of the development banks around the world, that Canadians are basically generous when it comes to helping those who are in worse straits than themselves. This is true across society, including those who are poor in Canada.
Referring to the book entitled, "Common Crisis", the writers of it, under the chairmanship of Willy Brandt, identified the same thing about which I am talking, how people by themselves, one on one, in small non-governmental organizations have a natural desire to help other people. They have noticed this trait in other countries as well. One thing they proposed-and I would like to go on the record here as proposing it-is that Canada should join with other countries that have this powerful non-governmental orientation to see whether or not there should be an international body of non-governmental organizations around the world so that the direction and the work of these private agencies in communities throughout the world could be channelled through an international facility not unlike the IMF or the World Bank.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member a question with respect to the first part of his speech. I was unable to determine whether he was running for the job of a Cabinet Minister or a cardinal. I would like to know what makes the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) think that God is a socialist.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I would like to thank the Hon. Member for his very clear and quite obviously unbiased question. I assure him that I am not running for cardinal or for a Cabinet seat. I really do not think that God has voted recently. I am sure that on many occasions He must have a difficult time understanding the struggles of human beings.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Or she.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"Or she" as the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) just said. He must have a difficult time understanding how human beings struggle to solve the problems of the human condition.
I would like to relate my feelings to the Hon. Member. I learned about God in the Judeo-Christian tradition. My tradition-and I would expect his tradition-has come down through the Bible and the Judaic background of the Christian principles of the New Testament.
In my understanding of those books, beginning with the Old Testament, they clearly identify the role of a good Jew as being to love God with his whole heart, whole soul and whole mind and to love his neighbour with the same force. That was redefined by Jesus when He came to give us the principles of Christianity. In that tradition that is the way I understand God.
The words we use today to describe how people treat each other in economics vary. Some people lump it under the term "free enterprise". I would be glad to ask my colleague whether he would be willing to enter into a discussion on whether God is a free enterpriser. On the other hand, other people will lump the way men and women treat others under the term "Communism". I could ask anybody whether God is a Communist, and they could answer whatever they wanted. But according to my conscience and according to the way I understand what both charity and justice mean in the Christian tradition, I quite clearly believe that the socialist way of thinking about taking the creation of the world and distributing it in such a way that all people benefit from it is closer to my understanding of how God asks us to live our lives than are other principles which could be set out. I would be glad if the Hon. Member would rise and explain to me whether he thinks God is a free enterpriser.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the Hon. Member has reflected upon this very serious question in the past in view of what he has chosen to do in life.
Turning to the intervention of the Bishops in questions of the economy or questions of society generally, does the Hon. Member agree that when people make interventions with the authority of God, or are perceived by the public to be speaking with the authority of the church, it is important to draw a line between being an inspirational force for Catholics, all Christians or all members of society, and commenting, analyzing or criticizing the means used by Government, which really brings people into the political arena? I realize that the Hon. Member has chosen to be in the political arena. That is all right because
May 3, 1983

when he does that I believe he does not speak with the authority of God or of the church. Does he see the difference which I see clearly? If so, where does he think the line should be drawn?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) is definitely on target in the discussion that I initiated in my speech today. However, it is a little too complicated to answer fully in the time allotted to me.
First, let me say that the Bishops, in teaching people about morality, have the right to speak about the morality of any sector of the society. For example, they have the right to speak about the Hon. Member's marriage, whether or not he is living it properly. I believe they have a right to speak in areas concerning morality.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In public?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am just talking about different areas of peoples' lives which involve moral issues. There are moral issues involved in their personal lives and in their social lives. I believe the Bishops have the right to speak about the morality in the military. To speak about morality and put it into a kind of cloudy area has no meaning. They have to talk about what is going on. They have to risk talking about what is going on, even at the expense of being inaccurate in some of their appraisals. As a group of Canadians, people who are part and parcel of our society, in the same way that medical, industrial and labour people or any other group of society, they have a right to speak as Canadians, speaking from their base and from their authority on the questions of society, including the economy. It is easy to make judgments sometimes about particular moral events, but when it comes to the social fibre, the structures that oppress people in real situations, it is much more difficult to speak clearly, but it has to be spoken and spoken in the concrete.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have never heard the Member speak elsewhere. He knows what I mean. He is pretty good here at skirting a question. He has not answered my question. I was not asking about the right of the Bishops to speak. Everyone in this country has the right to speak; bishops, priests, members of Parliament and the public. There are no absolutes in this. It is a question of judgment and balance.
What is the Hon. Member's view as to where the line is drawn between being an inspirational force for society and discussing the means of Government, which is really politics? I am not asking him to talk about the rights of the Bishops or the wisdom of the Bishops. Everyone in this country has the right to speak. I am asking for his judgment as a politician who has been elected to this House on where the line should be drawn.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, what the Hon. Member said would give the impression that there are two camps in the world, one in which there is religion and one in which there is
The Budget

Mr. Fisher
not. I do not agree with that principle. I believe there is only one world, and that morality takes place throughout the world. If you are going to speak precisely about a moral question, you have to do it in the context of what is taking place. For that reason, I believe the Bishops have a right to speak about a moral question in the here and now.
The Member indicated that if they did so, they would lose their inspirational value. I challenge that. I feel the Bishops became much more inspirational to many more Christians in Canada because they spoke about the realities of what is going on. It may be that they did not inspire the Member because they spoke against what his Government is doing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Be serious.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am serious. I remember well the statement the Hon. Member made to the press. I feel that they, as well as other moral leaders, have a right to speak on that. Maybe the Hon. Member and I should continue this discussion outside the Chamber.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me finally to get a chance to talk on a budget that I have personally been involved with since the Minister started his pre-budget consultation last December with so many groups from the private sector.
As I listened to his decisions on budget night, I came to the conclusion that this budget is one that stresses fast action on job-creation, especially for those who need jobs the most. This is a budget that stresses rapid action by Government in key economic areas right across the country to get our recovery going. This is a budget that stresses relief for business to finance and to encourage their growth so that long-term recovery and long-term job-creation will be possible.
I personally welcome the considerable public support that we have heard since budget night. Let me quote a few examples from the private sector. In the area of small business, John

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
Bulloch, President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, was quoted by Canadian Press on April 19 as saying:
A combination of good politics and sound economics. Business will generally give high marks.
Mr. John Kyle of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce was quoted in The Gazette of April 20 as saying:
It sounds as if he listened to the business community.
Mr. Brian Aune of the Investment Dealers Association of Canada said:
A carefully thought out program to help the private sector in the recovery.
On jobs, another issue that has been contentious in this debate, let us listen to our constituents. Mr. Norman Godfrey of the Housing and Urban Development Association, a good Torontonian, is quoted in the April 20 Globe and Mail as having said:
The pro-business budget will generate confidence and create jobs.
Mr. Kenneth Nisbet of Westinghouse Canada Limited was quoted as follows in The Globe and Mail of April 21:
The Government's sudden attention to job-creation in the private sector is encouraging. It adds up to a better climate for the people who employ people.
John Grant, an investment economist, on the April 20 CTV National News said:
There is going to be a stronger expansion than we had guessed the night before the budget.
Pat Johnston of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business was quoted on CTV Canada AM as saying:
So on balance we are very pleased. People are now more confident. And confidence actually will create more jobs than tax breaks.
Those are important statements from the private sector on small business and jobs. When you look at a more general reaction to the budget, you get equally positive feedback. Terry Elder of the accounting firm of Deloitte Haskins and Sells is quoted in the April 26 Toronto Sun as follows:
It demonstrated Finance Minister Marc Lalonde is willing to listen-and act upon-the requests of the small business community.
In its editorial, the Ottawa Citizen on April 27 stated:
Evidence of Canada's economic recovery is mounting, and tends to confirm that the federal Government's approach in last week's budget was the right one.
Those are all positive comments from people in the private sector, key replies to some of the criticisms we have heard here.
How is it that this budget came about? I mentioned that I was involved in the consultation process from December onward. We met with representatives from every corner of the country, from every part of the private sector. I personally sat in on meetings with mayors, reeves, housing industry representatives, the Canadian Labour Congress, the co-operative and credit unions, small business, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Canadian Bankers' Association. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) canvassed as many representatives of Canadians as he could find. He listened to them. He took their ideas and threaded them together to create the budget. That, Mr. Speaker, is why we are now hearing so
many Canadians say that they approve the budget. He listened, he absorbed the ideas, he acted on them, and people are now gaining confidence in his decisions.
What did the people tell us during that long process? Well, first they told us not to be afraid of more Government spending, as long as it is wise spending. We got that input from both business and labour. We were encouraged to take up a program of permanent public works that would add to the wealth and the inventory of our country. We have done that. Take a look at what is contained in the budget. There are 100 projects that will stimulate key sectors from coast to coast. Look at the efforts in housing. Look at the efforts in construction. All of these will add up and create lasting monuments to our recovery.
Mr. Speaker, you and I know about the marvelous impact such efforts can have. For example, take a look from coast to coast at the heritage left from centennial year. What town, what corner of this country does not have a little library or a little monument to centennial year? In the same way, we are now embarking upon key efforts to stimulate the recovery with permanent public works.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is something that the private sector advised us to do, and we are doing it.
The second thing the private sector told us to do is to use tax incentives and to rely on the private sector, and especially to allow the private sector to alleviate its losses through the tax system. We have done that. Take a look at the $2.4 billion in tax incentives and growth incentives that are contained in the private sector portion of the budget. That $2.4 billion will make the recovery permanent for small and big business coast to coast. That was an idea that we received from the private sector and we acted on it.
Finally, the private sector told us that confidence and recovery would go hand in hand. Take a look at how the private sector has reacted since that time. Eric Owen of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in the April 23 Financial Post said, and I quote him proudly:
The Minister has done his homework and taken constructive criticism.
Barbara Morrison of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business said to the Vancouver Sun on April 20:
The most important thing about this budget is the attitude. It's the change of attitude that will give business encouragement.
Sam Hughes of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce said to the CBC program "Sunday Morning" on April 24:
We do have to offer him constructive balanced advice and as long as he keeps acting on it we're going to keep applauding.
Finally, returning to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, John Bulloch told the CBC program "The House" on April 23:
It's going to make our members feel more positive about the country, it's going to make them feel more positive about reinvestment.
May 3, 1983

That, Mr. Speaker, means that business will be more positive about growth and new opportunity and new jobs because the Government had listened to them. They are enthusiastic because, right from the beginning, we went to Canadians and listened to them. We heard their advice and acted on it.
The private sector is excited because we have given it a chance to recover and to recover permanently. We have given it a chance to expand and to create jobs and to go back to work. All Canadians join us in applauding that goal.
As I have said, there are three basic themes in this budget. One is to create work quickly for those people who do not have work now, and we have dedicated over $700 million in the budget above and beyond money already dedicated by previous budgets. So today we have a total of almost $1.5 billion dedicated to direct job creation.
We went to the private sector and asked them to start growing through tax incentives and through incentives for investment. That is the second part of our budget. $2.4 billion will go into that. As I mentioned, the public works program will start to accelerate the recovery in key areas right away, and $2.4 billion more will go into that.
What has the Opposition had to say about this? Frankly, I have listened to six days of debate here, debate that I believe has been kind of dispirited and disjointed. I do not see any real focus to the criticism. There are some points, however, that 1 would like to raise and answer right now.
The Tories, for example, have taken up their classic wail about the level of the deficit. In doing so, they have demanded that we cut Government spending despite the benefits I described that will be derived from that spending. Of course, we have heard a variety of voices over there, some saying, "Well, let us get busy and cut the deficit," and others saying, "Let us get busy and increase our programs". Well, having listened to all of that, I suppose we should take our advice from one of the leadership candidates, Mr. Michael Wilson from Etobicoke Centre, who said, as reported in the Globe and Mail-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the usual practice to refer to Hon. Members by their constituencies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Member for Etobicoke Centre, Mr. Speaker, and I stand corrected. I apologize for my error. The Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) said in the Globe and Mail two days ago that if he went to work at his very hardest, the best he could do is to get the deficit down to $29 billion. One does not know where those $2 billion would have been cut from. I suspect that if we were to follow the typical Tory example, those cuts would come from the backs of working Canadians.
Mr. Thomas Maxwell, from the prestigious Conference Board In Canada said to the CBC program "As It Happens" on April 20:
I can't see any major financial problems associated with the deficit or the projections they have in their budget.
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
I agree with Dr. Maxwell. I believe that the spending we have undertaken in the budget will be a key element in our recovery at this time. It was not done flippantly or carelessly. It was done to stimulate recovery and to use the great mechanism of the Government's influence to help lift the level of economic activity as swiftly as possible.
Another complaint we have heard from the Conservative benches, particularly from Members like the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn), is the great complaint that we are raising taxes. That complaint ignores the previous advice they gave us about cutting the deficit. It also ignores the fact that the tax increases we have in this budget will come at a time when the recovery is here and we will be able to afford the extra taxes. We are not implementing these taxes now when the recovery is still young. We will wait until it is in its full maturity, until people can afford to pay a bit extra. In late 1984 and early 1985, we will begin to ask for a little extra money to pay for the recovery that we will be enjoying then.
Equally, we have heard from our friends from the NDP the same kind of twisted logic. The Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) just told us that every Canadian has the right to work. This is a significant change from the debate that we have heard previously both from Members of that Party and other Members in the House. Previously we urged and fought for 50 years to give Canadians the support of their community when they cannot get work. That is a very important difference. Yet when we do find ways to create jobs through youth employment programs, summer programs, the NEED Program, how are these programs described by the NDP? They are described as a process of raking leaves as if efforts to create genuine work can be written off and demeaned by that kind of slander. I do not agree, Mr. Speaker.
In my riding the budget has brought a real benefit to consumers. In my riding the incentives offered in the RHOSP are going to stimulate home building and the furniture industry. Our home builders, developers, construction people and their employees are going to benefit from that new program.
I have received a letter from Erindale College, University of Toronto, written by Dr. Paul Fox, the Principal of that outstanding institution. As we know, the federal Government will put $290 million into 15 new research centres across the country. Dr. Fox writes:
I am glad to hear that the government is considering sponsoring fifteen high tech centres. Jeff Fawcett, the Dean of Science, and I would like to discuss the matter with you at your earliest convenience.
I will be happy to tell Dr. Fox that I will be pursuing one of those centres for Mississauga to complement the vigorous research industries there, with computers, the defence industry and in the electronics industry. I hope the Minister of Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) and his associate, the Hon. Member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) are listening because I want one of those centres in Mississauga, the heart of research and development in Canada.

May 3, 1983
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
In my riding jobs are a key issue. People see how we have stabilized business opportunities, the way we have put cash back into the hands of business and the way we have given them incentives to expand. These are the ways to create permanent jobs and that is welcomed.
Ordinary families in my riding welcome the high Child Tax Credit that has been continued. People in my riding welcome the high child care expense deduction at $2,000 per child. That is a welcome benefit for working parents in Mississauga and all across Canada. Ordinary working people in Mississauga welcome the higher work expense deduction so that people can claim either $500 or up to 20 per cent of taxable income.
Young people in my area want to join Katimavik. When the Streetsville Secondary School band played on the steps of Parliament Hill last week, members of the band asked me for application forms as several students wanted to work there for the year. Young people in my riding welcome the higher student loans. They welcome the extra money for Summer Canada. They are glad to see the Youth Internship Program and the extra opportunity in the Armed Forces.
Above all, Mr. Speaker, families in Mississauga and across Canada welcome the extra money in direct job creation. In my city we have seen improvements made to our parks. We have seen a new computer program brought into the library system. Co-operative housing has been upgraded. Private business is starting to take advantage of NEED grants. All of this is happening in Mississauga, and it is typical of the job-creation programs that are going on from coast to coast.
I should like to conclude by quoting a comment made by Dr. William Mackness, chief economist of the Bank of Nova Scotia who said:
I think that there is a tremendous amount of pent-up demand in the North American economy. We've not built enough automobiles, appliances, homes now for several years. The biggest impediment, I think, in the way of a long and sustained recovery is the level of interest rates. They are too high. I'm optimistic that they'll come down considerably, and on that basis. I'd look forward to a long vigorous, sustained recovery.
[ Translation]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
